options.rationale: Urine sitting still allows infection and stone formation, which is how stasis presents.

options.text: A specific gravity of 1.015
options.rationale: Within the normal range and not a sign of stasis.

questions.takeaway: Urinary stasis raises infection risk and allows stones to form.

questions.stem: A patient in traction cannot move the affected leg but is able to exercise the other limbs. Which exercise maintains strength in the immobilized leg?

options.text: Isotonic exercise, contracting the muscle while the joint moves
options.rationale: Requires joint movement, which traction prevents.

options.text: Passive range of motion performed by the nurse
options.rationale: Maintains flexibility. The patient's muscle does no work, so no strength is built.

options.text: Resistance training with ankle weights
options.rationale: Adds load through a moving joint, which is not possible or safe here.

options.text: Isometric exercise, contracting the muscle without moving the joint
options.rationale: Builds static strength and joint stability and is safe around painful or healing tissue.

questions.takeaway: Isotonic moves the joint. Isometric does not, which is why it works in a limb that must stay still.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing factors that influence a patient's level of activity. Which factor does not influence a patient's level of activity?

options.text: Social support
options.rationale: Determines whether someone has help and encouragement to stay active.

options.text: Blood type
options.rationale: Has no relationship to activity or mobility.

options.text: Environment
options.rationale: Stairs, terrain and access decide what movement is possible.

options.text: Culture
options.rationale: Shapes which activities are valued and considered appropriate.

questions.takeaway: Activity is shaped by development, health status, lifestyle, culture, environment, behavior and social support.
questions.strategy: The word not flips the question. Three options are real influences on activity. Pick the one that has nothing to do with movement.

steps.detail: You are looking for the factor that does not belong.
Support, environment and culture all change what a person does.
Blood type has no link to activity.

elimination.verdict: B, blood type.

questions.stem: A patient recovering from pneumonia has been in bed for four days. Which action best prevents respiratory complications of immobility?

options.text: Assist the patient to sit upright and cough and deep breathe
options.rationale: Sitting upright increases lung expansion and coughing clears retained secretions, which are the two failures behind atelectasis.

options.text: Apply sequential compression devices to both legs
options.rationale: Prevents venous stasis and thrombus. It does nothing for the lungs.

options.text: Perform passive range of motion to all extremities
options.rationale: Prevents contractures. Correct care, different system.

options.text: Increase dietary protein intake
options.rationale: Addresses negative nitrogen balance, not lung expansion.

questions.takeaway: Match the intervention to the mechanism. Secretions pooling needs expansion and coughing.

questions.stem: A patient on bed rest for four days is preparing to ambulate. Supine blood pressure is 128/76 with a pulse of 78. After sitting at the edge of the bed for one minute, blood pressure is 102/58 with a pulse of 104 and the patient reports the room is spinning. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Assist the patient to stand so the episode resolves with movement
options.rationale: Standing raises the head further above the heart and deepens the drop in cerebral perfusion. This is the moment a fall happens.

options.text: Keep the patient sitting and supported, then recheck before standing
options.rationale: A drop in pressure with a compensating rise in rate on sitting is orthostatic hypotension. Staying seated lets the circulation catch up without abandoning the activity, and the recheck is the checkpoint before the riskiest part.

options.text: Return the patient to supine and cancel activity for the day
options.rationale: Abandoning the activity treats the symptom by deepening the deconditioning that caused it.

options.text: Administer the ordered analgesic and reattempt in one hour
options.rationale: Nothing in the findings describes pain, and an hour of additional rest does not improve orthostatic tolerance.

questions.takeaway: Read the pair together: falling pressure with a rising rate on position change is orthostatic hypotension. Stage the change, do not cancel it.

questions.stem: A patient has been immobile for five days after a pelvic fracture. The nurse notes that the left calf is 3 cm larger than the right and is warm and tender. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Apply the sequential compression devices to both legs
options.rationale: Compression prevents venous stasis in a limb without a clot. Applying it now treats prevention as if it were treatment.

options.text: Encourage active ankle pumping in both legs every hour
options.rationale: Leg exercises are correct prevention and are not the response to a limb that already shows the complication.

options.text: Hold the sequential compression devices and notify the provider
options.rationale: Unilateral calf swelling with warmth and tenderness suggests a thrombus has already formed. Compression on a limb with a suspected clot is applied only after evaluation, so the device is held and the finding is reported.

options.text: Measure both calves again in four hours to establish a trend
options.rationale: The difference is already measured and symptomatic. Waiting adds risk without adding information.

questions.takeaway: Prevention and treatment are different. Once one limb shows swelling, warmth, and tenderness, stop preventing and start reporting.

questions.stem: A patient who slides down in bed several times a day has an area of reddened, partially denuded skin over the sacrum. The bed is routinely kept at 45 degrees. Which change most directly addresses the mechanism causing this injury?

options.text: Apply a moisture barrier ointment to the sacrum twice daily
options.rationale: Moisture management is appropriate skin care and does nothing about the sliding that is tearing tissue.

options.text: Turn the patient every two hours without changing the bed angle
options.rationale: Turning limits time under pressure. The injury here is produced by sliding, which continues at 45 degrees.

options.text: Place a pillow under the knees to improve comfort
options.rationale: Knee flexion does help resist sliding, and alone it does not address either the bed angle or how the patient is moved.

options.text: Lower the head of the bed when clinically possible and use a lift sheet to reposition
options.rationale: Elevation lets the skeleton slide while the skin stays fixed, which is shear, and dragging adds friction. Lowering the angle removes the driving force and lifting removes the surface drag.

questions.takeaway: Pressure pushes down, friction rubs, shear slides the tissue under fixed skin. A head-up bed plus dragging produces the last two.

questions.stem: A patient immobile for two weeks has a footboard in place. The nurse finds the feet resting with the toes pointed and a gap of several inches between the soles and the board. Which conclusion does the nurse draw?

options.text: The device is not in contact with the feet, so it is not preventing plantar flexion
options.rationale: A footboard works only when the soles rest against it at a neutral angle. A gap means the ankles are free to settle into plantar flexion, which is how foot drop develops.

options.text: The findings are expected and the device is working as intended
options.rationale: Toes pointed is the position the device exists to prevent, so the finding is evidence it is not working.

options.text: The patient has developed a permanent contracture that the device can now correct
options.rationale: Contractures are permanent shortening. Positioning prevents them and does not reverse them, and nothing here establishes one has formed yet.

options.text: The gap indicates the patient has been performing active ankle exercises
options.rationale: Active movement would show the ankles in varied positions, not both settled in plantar flexion.

questions.takeaway: A supportive device only works in contact. Check that the intervention is actually happening, not just present.

questions.stem: A patient immobile for three weeks eats about a third of each meal. Serum albumin has fallen from 3.8 to 2.9 g/dL, weight is down 4 kg, and the arms and legs appear visibly thinner. Which process best explains this pattern?

options.text: Fluid volume deficit producing the weight loss
options.rationale: Dehydration would raise albumin through hemoconcentration rather than lower it, and it does not thin the extremities.

options.text: Negative nitrogen balance from immobility compounded by reduced intake
options.rationale: Immobility drives protein breakdown beyond intake, and decreased appetite is itself a listed metabolic effect. Falling albumin with visible loss of lean mass is that process made measurable.

options.text: Increased metabolic demand from prolonged bed rest
options.rationale: Immobility lowers metabolic demand. The direction is reversed.

options.text: Altered calcium metabolism causing muscle wasting
options.rationale: Altered calcium metabolism produces bone demineralization and a rising serum calcium, not loss of muscle protein.

questions.takeaway: Immobility takes protein apart while appetite falls. Albumin down, weight down, limbs thinner is one process, not three.

questions.stem: A patient two days after knee arthroplasty is on a weight-bearing restriction and reports the knee is too painful to bend beyond a few degrees. Which exercise best maintains quadriceps strength now?

options.text: Perform straight leg raises through the full range
options.rationale: Isotonic work through a full arc. The hip moves and the load on a painful healing knee exceeds what this patient tolerates.

options.text: Have the nurse move the knee through its full range twice daily
options.rationale: Passive range maintains flexibility and the patient's muscle does no work, so no strength is built.

options.text: Tighten the quadriceps and hold without moving the knee
options.rationale: Isometric contraction loads the muscle with no joint movement, which is why it is used around painful or healing joints. Strength and joint stability are preserved during the period the knee cannot move.

options.text: Walk short distances with a walker several times daily
options.rationale: Isotonic and appropriate later. It conflicts with the weight-bearing restriction stated in the stem.

questions.takeaway: Isotonic moves the joint, isometric does not. When the joint cannot move, isometric is the only way to keep the muscle.

questions.stem: A nurse repositions an immobile patient from supine to a 30-degree side-lying position with pillows supporting the back, between the knees and under the upper arm. Which statement about this positioning requires correction?

options.text: It maintains body alignment
options.rationale: Accurate. Support at the back, knees and arm holds the trunk and limbs in alignment instead of letting them collapse into the mattress.

options.text: It reduces pressure over the sacrum
options.rationale: Accurate. Turning shifts weight off the tissue that was bearing it, which limits time under load.

options.text: It supports lung expansion compared with a flat supine position
options.rationale: Accurate. Position determines how far the lungs can expand. Turning off the back lets the chest wall and the upper lung expand more freely than lying flat.

options.text: It eliminates the need for scheduled range-of-motion exercises
options.rationale: Position and movement do different jobs. Holding a joint correctly does not carry it through its arc.

questions.takeaway: Positioning maintains alignment, supports breathing, protects skin, promotes comfort, prevents contractures and supports function. It does not replace movement.
questions.strategy: The stem asks for the false statement. The word eliminates is an absolute that no single intervention earns.

steps.detail: Look for the outcome positioning cannot deliver.
Each follows from the pillows and the turn.
Eliminates claims position can stand in for movement.

elimination.verdict: D. Positioning does not replace range of motion.

questions.scenario: A 79-year-old is on day 2 of an admission for a heart failure exacerbation. Furosemide 40 mg by mouth is scheduled at 1000 and 2200. Overnight the patient voided five times between 2300 and 0500. Staff found the patient walking to the bathroom alone twice. Once there was urine on the floor beside the bed. The patient has been alert and oriented x4 on every check. Glasses are on and within reach. Orthostatic vital signs at 0600: lying 132/78 with a pulse of 80, standing 128/76 with a pulse of 84, no dizziness. Weight is down 1.1 kg from yesterday. The fall risk score is high.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 risk factor the plan must target, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Schedule toileting every 1 to 2 hours overnight with assistive personnel
options.rationale: Getting the patient to the bathroom before the urge peaks removes the reason to rush. The deck pairs urgency with scheduled toileting every 1 to 2 hours.

options.text: Ask the provider and pharmacist whether the evening furosemide dose can be given earlier in the day
options.rationale: The 2200 dose is producing diuresis all night. Moving it earlier keeps the benefit and moves the voiding to hours when the patient is awake and staff are nearby.

options.text: Place a bed alarm and tell the patient to stay in bed until morning
options.rationale: An alarm tells you after the patient is already up. Telling someone with urgency to stay in bed sets up another solo trip or incontinence.

options.text: Reorient the patient to the room every hour overnight
options.rationale: This targets confusion. The patient has been oriented on every check, so it does not touch the actual risk.

options.text: Hold the 2200 furosemide dose tonight
options.rationale: Holding a prescribed diuretic in heart failure is not a nursing fall intervention. Timing changes go through the provider and pharmacist.

options.text: Urinary urgency and frequency from diuretic timing
options.rationale: Five voids overnight after a 2200 diuretic dose, solo trips and urine on the floor. The patient is rushing to the bathroom.

options.text: Medication-related dizziness
options.rationale: The orthostatic check is negative and there is no dizziness. The medication is causing urgency, not unsteadiness.

options.text: Confusion and disorientation
options.rationale: Oriented x4 on every check.

options.text: Visual impairment
options.rationale: Glasses are on and within reach.

options.text: Number of times the patient gets up alone overnight
options.rationale: This is the unsafe behavior the plan is meant to stop. If it keeps happening the plan is not working.

options.text: Nighttime voiding frequency after the dose timing changes
options.rationale: Shows whether moving the dose shifted the diuresis out of the night.

options.text: Orientation score each shift
options.rationale: Worth charting routinely. It does not measure the risk factor being treated.

options.text: Orthostatic blood pressure every 4 hours
options.rationale: Already negative. Repeating it every 4 hours overnight adds sleep disruption without measuring the target.

questions.takeaway: Match the intervention to the actual risk factor. Urgency is handled with scheduled toileting and, when a diuretic drives it, with a conversation about dose timing.
questions.strategy: The scenario rules out confusion, vision and dizziness with specific data. Use each negative finding to cross off an option, then pick the actions that fit what is left.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Rule out the other risk factors
steps.detail: Oriented x4, glasses on, orthostatics negative.
Five overnight voids after a 2200 diuretic mean urgency.
Scheduled toileting and a timing review. Reject alarms, bed rest and holding the drug.
Solo trips out of bed and nighttime voiding.

elimination.verdict: Urgency from diuretic timing; scheduled toileting and a timing review; solo trips and nighttime voids.

questions.stem: At 0300 a nurse finds an 81-year-old on the floor beside the bed. The patient takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. The patient is awake, says "I just wanted to get to the bathroom," and is trying to push up to stand. There is a small red area on the forehead. The nurse has called for assistance without leaving the patient. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Return the patient to bed with enough staff and the correct lift equipment
options.rationale: Safe patient handling is right, but only after injury is ruled in or out. Moving first can turn a hip fracture or a neck injury into something worse.

options.text: Notify the provider of the fall and the anticoagulant
options.rationale: A fall on an anticoagulant can bleed slowly, so the provider needs to know. The call comes after you have assessment findings to report.

options.text: Assess for injury, including the head, hips and level of consciousness, before moving the patient
options.rationale: You find out what is hurt before you move anyone. The anticoagulant and the forehead mark make a head injury the thing you are looking for.

options.text: Document the event factually and complete the occurrence report
options.rationale: Last in the deck sequence. The chart records what you found and did. The occurrence report goes to risk management and is not mentioned in the chart.

questions.takeaway: After a fall: get help and stay, assess before you move, move safely, notify, fix the plan, then document.
questions.strategy: The patient trying to stand is the pull toward helping them up right away. Every option is a correct action. Only one belongs right after calling for help.

steps.detail: "Next" means help is already on the way.
Head, hips and consciousness come before any transfer.
Move safely, then notify the provider. Documentation comes last.

elimination.verdict: C. Assess for injury before moving the patient.

questions.stem: At 2300 the nurse assesses a 76-year-old on day 2 after surgical repair of a right hip fracture. She is pulling at the IV and trying to climb out of bed. Last oxycodone was given at 1500. She grimaces when the right leg is moved. She last voided at 1600. The lower abdomen is firm and rounded above the pubis. Diphenhydramine 50 mg was given at 2130 for sleep. She is oriented to person only. She was oriented x3 at 1400. The overhead light and television are on. Her roommate's visitors are talking loudly. Oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. Blood pressure is 138/82. The surgical dressing is dry and intact. Assistive personnel ask the nurse for wrist restraints. Which action by the nurse is best?

options.text: Obtain a provider order for wrist restraints to protect the IV
options.rationale: Pulling at the IV is the behavior you are trying to explain. A restraint is a last resort after causes and alternatives. It does not treat pain or a full bladder. It can increase agitation and confusion.

options.text: Raise all four side rails so she cannot climb out of bed
options.rationale: Four raised rails act as a restraint. A confused patient who wants to toilet or escape pain often climbs over a rail, which causes a fall.

options.text: Assess her pain and bladder, then give the due analgesic and help her empty her bladder
options.rationale: Eight hours since analgesia on the second day after hip surgery, plus seven hours without voiding and a palpable bladder. Pain and a full bladder are fixable causes that look like agitation. The diphenhydramine may explain both the new disorientation and the retention. Addressing causes comes before a restraint.

options.text: Ask the provider for a sedative so she will sleep through the night
options.rationale: A drug given to control behavior is a chemical restraint. Another sedating drug in an older adult with new disorientation can deepen delirium, just as the diphenhydramine may already have.

questions.takeaway: Before a restraint, ask why. Pain, a full bladder, a medication effect, delirium and overstimulation are all fixable. Fixing them often ends the behavior.
questions.strategy: The request for restraints frames the question as a safety problem. Three options control the behavior. Only one looks for its cause. Walk the deck's list of causes and match each one to a finding.

steps.detail: Pulling and climbing is what you are explaining.
Wrist restraints, four rails and a sedative all restrict her. They are physical or chemical restraints.
Only C assesses and treats a cause: pain and a full bladder.

elimination.verdict: C.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old admitted for pneumonia was started on a new antihypertensive at 0900. The patient is oriented x4 and continent. She walked independently at home. At 1000 lying blood pressure is 136/80 and standing blood pressure is 108/64. She says she feels lightheaded and sits back down. At 1400 standing blood pressure is 128/76 with no symptoms. Which intervention best targets this patient's fall risk?

options.text: Assist with mobility in the hours after each dose and review the dose timing with the pharmacist
options.rationale: The drop appears within an hour of the first dose and resolves by afternoon, which points to the drug. This matches the deck: monitor symptoms, adjust timing and assist with mobility. It protects her when the risk is highest without taking away her independence the rest of the day.

options.text: Keep her on bed rest until the medication is discontinued
options.rationale: Bed rest causes weakness and deconditioning, which adds a second fall risk factor. Staying in bed would make the next fall more likely.

options.text: Raise all four side rails while she is in bed
options.rationale: Four rails are a restraint and increase injury when patients climb over them. The deck prohibits restraints for routine fall prevention.

options.text: Reorient her to the room every hour
options.rationale: Targets confusion, which she does not have. She is oriented x4.

questions.takeaway: Read the trend. A drop that tracks the dose time and then resolves is a medication effect. You plan around the dose instead of taking away mobility.
questions.strategy: The 1400 reading is the tie breaker. It is normal, which tells you the problem is tied to a time window, not to the patient all day.

steps.detail: Drop an hour after the dose, gone by afternoon. The risk factor is medication-related dizziness.
Bed rest and four rails create new risk.
Reorienting targets confusion she does not have.

elimination.verdict: A. Assist after doses and review the timing.

questions.stem: A nurse is working with assistive personnel on a unit where several patients are on individualized fall prevention plans. Which activity may the nurse delegate to assistive personnel?

options.text: Decide whether a patient who now walks steadily can move from one-person assist to standby assist
options.rationale: Changing the level of assistance changes the plan. Determining the prevention plan belongs to the RN.

options.text: Review the past two nights to decide whether scheduled toileting reduced solo trips out of bed
options.rationale: This is evaluation. Judging whether the plan worked is an RN step.

options.text: Help the patient to the chair using the gait belt and walker listed in the plan
options.rationale: Assisting with mobility according to the plan is delegable. The words according to the plan are what make it delegable.

options.text: Recalculate the fall risk score after a new sedative is started
options.rationale: Assessing fall risk is an RN responsibility. A new sedative is a change that calls for reassessment.

questions.takeaway: The RN assesses fall risk, builds the plan and evaluates it. Assistive personnel carry out the plan, keep the room safe and report what they see.
questions.strategy: Look for the verb hidden in each option. Decide, review and recalculate are judgment. Help with the device listed in the plan is a task inside a plan someone else made.

steps.detail: Decide, review whether it worked, recalculate.
Help the patient with the device listed in the plan.
Changing the level of assist looks like mobility help. It is a plan change.

elimination.verdict: C is the only task carried out inside an existing plan.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has an arterial blood gas showing pH 7.36, PaCO2 58 mm Hg, and HCO3 32 mEq/L. How does the nurse interpret this result?

options.text: Normal blood gas, no action needed
options.rationale: The pH is normal and nothing else is. Two abnormal values with a normal pH is the signature of compensation, not health.

options.text: Fully compensated respiratory acidosis
options.rationale: The CO2 is high, which acidifies. The bicarbonate is high, which is the kidney buffering it. The pH has been pulled back inside the range, so compensation is complete.

options.text: Partially compensated metabolic alkalosis
options.rationale: A metabolic alkalosis would start with a raised bicarbonate and a raised pH. The pH is not alkalotic and the CO2 elevation is the primary problem, not the compensation.

options.text: Uncompensated respiratory acidosis
options.rationale: Uncompensated means the pH is still abnormal and the metabolic value is still normal. Here the bicarbonate has already moved and the pH has come back.

questions.takeaway: A pH inside the normal range with an abnormal CO2 and an abnormal bicarbonate is full compensation, and it means a chronic problem underneath.
questions.strategy: The normal pH is bait. Read the other two numbers before you decide the patient is fine.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It is 7.36, normal but sitting on the acidic side of 7.40.
58 is high, so the lung is the problem and the direction is acidosis.
32 is high, moving opposite the pH, which makes it compensation.

elimination.verdict: Respiratory acidosis, fully compensated. A normal pH does not mean a normal patient.

questions.stem: A patient has been vomiting for three days. Which acid-base disturbance does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Metabolic acidosis
options.rationale: Metabolic acidosis comes from losing bicarbonate below the stomach, which is diarrhea, or from gaining acid, which is ketoacidosis or renal failure.

options.text: Metabolic alkalosis
options.rationale: Gastric contents are hydrochloric acid. Vomiting removes acid from the body, so what is left is relatively alkaline.

options.text: Respiratory acidosis
options.rationale: Respiratory problems change the CO2. Vomiting does not affect ventilation directly.

options.text: Respiratory alkalosis
options.rationale: Respiratory alkalosis comes from blowing off CO2, which is hyperventilation, not vomiting.

questions.takeaway: Vomiting loses acid and causes alkalosis. Diarrhea loses bicarbonate and causes acidosis. They are opposites and they are tested as a pair.
questions.strategy: Two options are metabolic and two are respiratory. The stem gives you a gastrointestinal loss, so the metabolic pair is where the answer lives.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Metabolic versus respiratory. Vomiting is not a breathing problem.
Stomach contents are acid.
Lose acid, become alkalotic.

elimination.verdict: Metabolic alkalosis. The mirror item gives you diarrhea and the answer flips to acidosis.

questions.stem: Which assessment gives the nurse the most reliable early evidence that a patient with heart failure is retaining fluid?

options.text: Daily weight taken at the same time on the same scale
options.rationale: A liter of fluid weighs about one kilogram, or 2.2 pounds. The scale registers the gain before edema is visible and before crackles appear.

options.text: Presence of pitting edema in the ankles
options.rationale: Edema is real but late. Several liters can accumulate before the tissue shows it, and dependent edema also varies with position and time of day.

options.text: Crackles heard in the lung bases
options.rationale: Crackles mean fluid has already reached the lungs. That is a finding you act on, not an early warning.

options.text: Patient report of thirst and dry mouth
options.rationale: Thirst points toward deficit rather than excess, and thirst is unreliable in older adults because the thirst mechanism blunts with age.

questions.takeaway: Weight is the honest number. One kilogram equals one liter, and the scale changes before edema or crackles do. Same time, same scale, same clothing.
questions.strategy: Three options are findings that appear after the fluid has already collected. Only one of them catches it on the way in.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Ask which finding appears first.
Both are late and both require a volume that has already accumulated.
It points the wrong direction and it is unreliable in older adults.

elimination.verdict: Daily weight. It is the earliest and the most reproducible.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old is admitted from home after two days of poor oral intake in a heat wave. Heart rate is 112 and blood pressure is 96/58. Urine output is 15 mL/hr, dark and concentrated. She has lost 3 kg since last week. The skin on the back of her hand tents. Which finding is the least reliable evidence of fluid volume deficit in this patient?

options.text: Heart rate 112 and blood pressure 96/58
options.rationale: The earliest compensation for a falling volume is tachycardia. The blood pressure drops once compensation is exhausted.

options.text: Urine output 15 mL/hr, dark and concentrated
options.rationale: Below 30 mL/hr is oliguria. The kidney is conserving everything it can. Concentrating the urine is how it does that.

options.text: Weight loss of 3 kg since last week
options.rationale: Three kilograms is about three liters. Acute weight change is fluid, not tissue.

options.text: Tenting of the skin on the back of the hand
options.rationale: Aging skin tents on the hand and forearm whether or not the patient is dry. Assess turgor over the sternum or the forehead instead.

questions.takeaway: Deficit shows up as tachycardia first, then hypotension, with concentrated low-volume urine, acute weight loss and new confusion. Hand turgor and thirst are both unreliable in older adults.
questions.strategy: The stem asks for the least reliable finding. The wrong site for turgor is written to look like good assessment skill.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the one finding that does not prove deficit in an 82-year-old.

steps.action: Keep the vital signs and the urine
steps.detail: Both fit a falling circulating volume.
Acute change of this size is water.
Aging hand skin tents in anyone.

elimination.verdict: D. Hand turgor is the wrong site for an older adult.

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews the intravenous fluids prescribed for four patients on a medical unit.
questions.stem: For each fluid, indicate its tonicity relative to plasma.

rows.text: 0.9% sodium chloride, prescribed after several hours of vomiting
rows.rationale: Same osmolality as plasma, so it produces no net shift and stays in the space you infuse it into. That is what a patient who lost extracellular fluid needs.

rows.text: 0.45% sodium chloride, prescribed for cellular dehydration
rows.rationale: Lower osmolality than plasma, so water moves into the cells. Useful for rehydrating cells and dangerous in anyone at risk of cerebral edema.

rows.text: 3% sodium chloride, prescribed for symptomatic hyponatremia with seizures
rows.rationale: Higher osmolality than plasma, so it pulls water out of the cells. Given slowly and with close monitoring, because correcting sodium quickly causes osmotic demyelination.

rows.text: Lactated Ringer solution, prescribed for a patient with burns
rows.rationale: An isotonic balanced crystalloid. It expands the circulating volume without shifting fluid across the cell membrane.

questions.takeaway: Isotonic stays put and expands the vascular space. Hypotonic moves water into cells. Hypertonic pulls water out of them.
questions.strategy: Sort by the percentage against 0.9%, which is the isotonic reference. Below it moves water in, above it pulls water out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: That is isotonic, and so is lactated Ringer.
Less than 0.9% is hypotonic, more than 0.9% is hypertonic.
Cellular dehydration needs water in; cerebral edema needs water out.

elimination.verdict: Two isotonic, one hypotonic, one hypertonic.

questions.stem: A nurse receives an order reading: potassium chloride 20 mEq IV push now for a serum potassium of 2.9 mEq/L. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Administer it slowly over five minutes with the patient on a monitor
options.rationale: The trap. Administering a lethal route more carefully does not make it safe. There is no safe rate for IV push potassium.

options.text: Dilute it and infuse it over one hour through a peripheral line
options.rationale: Wrong twice. Diluting is the right idea and 20 mEq over one hour is 20 mEq/hr, double the peripheral maximum of 10 mEq/hr. Rewriting an unsafe order is also prescribing, which is not the nurse's to do.

options.text: Hold the dose and contact the prescriber to clarify the order
options.rationale: Potassium is never given IV push. The nurse who recognizes an unsafe order stops and questions it, and carrying out an unsafe order does not transfer the responsibility.

options.text: Give it orally instead, since the patient can swallow
options.rationale: Changing the route is prescribing. The recognition is correct and the action exceeds the nurse's scope.

questions.takeaway: IV push potassium is fatal. The correct response to an unsafe order is to question it, never to carry it out more carefully or to substitute your own version.
questions.strategy: Three options all find a way to give the drug. Only one of them stops.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Potassium is never pushed.
A slower push and a nurse-chosen dilution are both still acting on an unsafe order.
That is prescribing.

elimination.verdict: Hold and clarify. Reject the rate, not the technique.

questions.stem: Fifteen minutes into a unit of packed red blood cells, a patient develops chills, a temperature rise from 37.0 C to 38.6 C, and low back pain. What does the nurse do first?

options.text: Slow the infusion and continue to monitor
options.rationale: Slowing keeps incompatible blood going in. Every minute of continued infusion adds to the hemolysis.

options.text: Stop the transfusion and keep the line open with normal saline using new tubing
options.rationale: Stop first. Then maintain access with saline through fresh tubing, because running saline through the existing set would push the blood remaining in the line into the patient.

options.text: Administer the prescribed acetaminophen for the fever
options.rationale: Treats a symptom of a reaction that is still running. The drug never comes before stopping the cause.

options.text: Obtain a urine specimen to check for hemoglobinuria
options.rationale: It will be needed, and it is not first. Collecting a specimen while the transfusion continues is assessment at the expense of the patient.

questions.takeaway: When something goes wrong during an infusion or a transfusion, the first action is always to stop it. Assess, notify and document all come after.
questions.strategy: All four options are things that happen during this event. The question is only about order.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Stop before you call.
Reducing an exposure is not removing it.

steps.action: Cut the drug and the specimen
steps.detail: Both are correct later and neither is first.

elimination.verdict: Stop the transfusion, then saline through new tubing to the hub.

questions.stem: A patient in the emergency department is breathing 36 times a minute after a panic attack and reports tingling around the mouth and in both hands. Which explanation does the nurse give?

options.text: The calcium level has dropped and needs replacement
options.rationale: The total calcium has not changed. Alkalosis increases calcium binding to albumin, which lowers the ionized fraction without lowering the number on the lab report.

options.text: Rapid breathing has lowered the carbon dioxide and raised the blood pH
options.rationale: Hyperventilation blows off CO2, which produces respiratory alkalosis. Alkalosis shifts calcium onto albumin, and less free calcium means irritable nerves.

options.text: Oxygen levels have fallen and the tissues are hypoxic
options.rationale: Hyperventilation raises oxygen, it does not lower it. Nothing here suggests hypoxia.

options.text: Potassium has shifted out of the cells in response to stress
options.rationale: Alkalosis drives potassium into cells, not out. The direction is wrong and potassium does not cause perioral tingling.

questions.takeaway: Perioral and fingertip tingling appears in hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia and respiratory alkalosis. A hyperventilating patient with tingling lips has a breathing problem.
questions.strategy: Tingling is a strong cue for calcium, which is exactly why the question offers it. Read the respiratory rate before you reach for the electrolyte.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 36 a minute is the finding the stem is built on.
Fast breathing raises oxygen.
Alkalosis moves potassium in, not out.
The number has not changed, the binding has.

elimination.verdict: Respiratory alkalosis. The calcium option is the trap and it is the one most students pick.

questions.stem: Which condition would the nurse expect to produce metabolic acidosis?

options.text: Continuous nasogastric suction
options.rationale: Suction removes gastric acid, the same as vomiting. That produces alkalosis.

options.text: Prolonged hyperventilation from anxiety
options.rationale: That is a respiratory cause. It produces alkalosis by removing CO2.

options.text: Prolonged severe diarrhea
options.rationale: Intestinal contents below the stomach are alkaline. Losing them loses bicarbonate.

options.text: Chronic lung disease with CO2 retention
options.rationale: Retained CO2 does cause acidosis. The mechanism is the lungs, so it is respiratory acidosis rather than metabolic.

questions.takeaway: Metabolic acidosis comes from gaining fixed acid or losing bicarbonate. Ketones, lactate and retained renal acid are gains; diarrhea is the loss.
questions.strategy: Two options are respiratory and one is alkalosis in disguise. The gastrointestinal pair is the real test: diarrhea loses base while suction loses acid.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hyperventilation and CO2 retention are lung mechanisms. Remove both.
Suction, like vomiting, loses acid. Diarrhea loses base.

steps.action: Ask gained acid or lost base
steps.detail: Losing bicarbonate leaves the blood acidic.

elimination.verdict: C. Diarrhea loses bicarbonate. Nasogastric suction is the mirror image and produces alkalosis.

questions.stem: Complete each interpretation by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A patient with sepsis has pH 7.28, PaCO2 32 mm Hg, HCO3 15 mEq/L. This is [[1]].

A postoperative patient who has been receiving opioids has pH 7.30, PaCO2 54 mm Hg, HCO3 25 mEq/L. This is [[2]].

A patient with three days of nasogastric suction has pH 7.50, PaCO2 42 mm Hg, HCO3 32 mEq/L. This is [[3]].

For the septic patient, the respiratory rate of 30 is best understood as [[4]].

options.text: metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
options.rationale: The bicarbonate is low, which is the primary problem, and the pH is acidotic. The low CO2 is the lung blowing off acid to help.

options.text: respiratory acidosis
options.rationale: The CO2 is low, not high. A respiratory acidosis requires retained CO2.

options.text: metabolic alkalosis
options.rationale: The pH is 7.28, which is acidotic.

options.text: a fully compensated disturbance
options.rationale: Full compensation would have returned the pH to normal. It has not.

options.text: respiratory acidosis
options.rationale: The CO2 is high and the pH is low, moving opposite each other, which makes it respiratory. The normal bicarbonate means the kidney has not compensated yet.

options.text: metabolic acidosis
options.rationale: The bicarbonate is normal, so the metabolic side is not the problem.

options.text: respiratory alkalosis
options.rationale: That would show a low CO2 and a high pH.

options.text: a normal blood gas
options.rationale: A pH of 7.30 is below the range.

options.text: metabolic alkalosis
options.rationale: Suction removes gastric acid. The bicarbonate is high and the pH is high, and the CO2 is normal, so the metabolic side is the problem.

options.text: respiratory alkalosis
options.rationale: The CO2 is 42, which is normal. A respiratory alkalosis requires a low CO2.

options.text: metabolic acidosis
options.rationale: The pH is 7.50, which is alkalotic.

options.text: compensated respiratory acidosis
options.rationale: Nothing here is acidotic and the CO2 is normal.

options.text: compensation that should not be slowed
options.rationale: The fast breathing is how the body is offloading acid. Sedating it or slowing it removes the only compensation the patient has.

options.text: a primary respiratory problem needing sedation
options.rationale: The lung is helping, not failing. Slowing it would drive the pH lower.

options.text: anxiety requiring reassurance and rebreathing
options.rationale: That applies to respiratory alkalosis from panic. This patient is acidotic.

options.text: an indication for immediate intubation
options.rationale: Nothing in the values shows a failing airway or failing ventilation.

questions.takeaway: Read the pH, then the CO2, then the bicarbonate. The value moving opposite the pH is the cause; the value moving with it is compensation.
questions.strategy: The last blank is the one that matters clinically. Fast breathing is a cause in respiratory alkalosis and a rescue in metabolic acidosis.

strategies: Match each part to what the stem gives

steps.detail: Acidotic or alkalotic decides half the answer before you read anything else.

steps.action: Find the value moving opposite the pH
steps.detail: That one is the cause.

steps.action: Ask what the other value is doing
steps.detail: Moving with the pH means it is compensating.

elimination.verdict: Metabolic acidosis, respiratory acidosis, metabolic alkalosis, and the fast breathing is compensation you protect rather than treat.

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews findings for a patient with a calcium of 7.6 mg/dL and a patient with a calcium of 12.4 mg/dL.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is associated with hypocalcemia or hypercalcemia.

rows.text: Carpal spasm when a blood pressure cuff is inflated
rows.rationale: Positive Trousseau sign. The nerves fire too easily.

rows.text: Constipation, anorexia and hypoactive bowel sounds
rows.rationale: Calcium slows the smooth muscle in the gut.

rows.text: Decreased deep tendon reflexes and lethargy
rows.rationale: Nerves need a stronger stimulus to respond.

rows.text: Abdominal cramping with diarrhea
rows.rationale: The gut is overexcitable.

rows.text: Swelling and warmth in one calf
rows.rationale: High calcium raises the risk of blood clots. Assess for a DVT.

rows.text: Prolonged QT interval
rows.rationale: The deck's ECG change for low calcium.

questions.takeaway: Calcium is the brake on the nerves. Low calcium means excitable: tetany, Trousseau and Chvostek signs, diarrhea, prolonged QT. High calcium means slow: weak, lethargic, constipated, with a clot risk.
questions.strategy: The calf row is the one students miss. Clotting is a hypercalcemia complication, because calcium is part of clotting.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Low calcium means excitable; high calcium means slow.
Diarrhea goes with low calcium; constipation goes with high calcium.
Calcium is a clotting factor, so high calcium means clot risk.

elimination.verdict: Hypo, hyper, hyper, hypo, hyper, hypo.

questions.stem: A nurse on a medical unit reviews causes and cellular effects of sodium imbalances. Which statement correctly links a cause to its sodium imbalance and its effect on cells?

options.text: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) causes hyponatremia. Water moves into cells and they swell.
options.rationale: The body holds too much water, which dilutes the sodium. The serum is dilute, so water moves toward the more concentrated inside of the cell.

options.text: Hyperaldosteronism causes hyponatremia. Water moves into cells and they swell.
options.rationale: Aldosterone holds on to sodium. The level rises, so this is a cause of hypernatremia.

options.text: Fever with profuse sweating and poor fluid intake for three days causes hyponatremia. Water leaves cells and they shrink.
options.rationale: Water is lost faster than sodium, so what remains is concentrated. That is hypernatremia. The cell effect fits hypernatremia, so the two halves do not match.

options.text: Large volumes of hypotonic IV fluid cause hypernatremia. Water leaves cells and they shrink.
options.rationale: Extra free water dilutes the serum. That causes hyponatremia. Cells swell rather than shrink.

questions.takeaway: Water follows sodium. Low sodium swells cells and high sodium shrinks them. The brain feels both first.
questions.strategy: Test both halves of every option. Too much water means low sodium and swollen cells. Too little water means high sodium and shrunken cells.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: SIADH and hypotonic fluid add water. Fever and sweating remove it. Aldosterone keeps sodium, so the level rises.

steps.action: Check the imbalance in each option
steps.detail: B, C and D each pair the cause with the wrong direction.
Water moves toward the higher concentration, so dilute serum swells cells.

elimination.verdict: A. SIADH causes hyponatremia with swollen cells.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with chronic kidney disease has been taking milk of magnesia every night for constipation. He is drowsy and hard to wake. Heart rate 52, blood pressure 90/56, respirations 11 and shallow. Patellar reflexes are absent. Serum magnesium is 4.6 mEq/L. Which plan of care is most appropriate?

options.text: Hypomagnesemia. Give IV magnesium sulfate. Place him in a dim, quiet room to prevent seizures. Monitor the Chvostek sign.
options.rationale: Low magnesium causes brisk reflexes and excitability. IV magnesium sulfate makes the toxicity worse.

options.text: Hypermagnesemia. Stop the milk of magnesia and every other magnesium source. Prepare IV calcium as prescribed. Monitor respiratory rate, depth and deep tendon reflexes.
options.rationale: Magnesium came in from the laxative. His kidneys cannot excrete it. Remove the source first. Calcium is the antidote because it counters magnesium's effect on the heart and the muscles. Respiratory failure is how high magnesium kills. Reflexes coming back is the early sign that the treatment is working.

options.text: Hypermagnesemia. Stop the milk of magnesia and every other magnesium source. Place him in a dim, quiet room to prevent seizures. Monitor the Chvostek sign.
options.rationale: The problem is right but the plan is not. Seizure precautions are for low magnesium. He is sedated, not excitable. The Chvostek sign is used for low calcium and low magnesium.

options.text: Hyperkalemia. Prepare IV calcium as prescribed. Monitor blood glucose.
options.rationale: Kidney disease fits. Absent reflexes with a magnesium of 4.6 do not. Blood glucose is not affected here.

questions.takeaway: Kidney failure plus a magnesium laxative or antacid means magnesium toxicity. Stop the source and give calcium. Watch the breathing and the reflexes.
questions.strategy: Seizure precautions sound safe. They belong to low magnesium. Choosing them means you picked the wrong direction. Check every part of the plan, not only the problem.

steps.detail: Kidney failure plus a magnesium laxative points to hypermagnesemia. That removes A and D.
Absent reflexes, bradycardia and slow breathing mean sedated, not excitable. That removes the seizure plan in C.

steps.action: Monitor what kills and what recovers first
steps.detail: Breathing and reflexes.

elimination.verdict: B. Hypermagnesemia; stop magnesium and give calcium; monitor respirations and reflexes.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old is admitted with heart failure and receives IV furosemide 40 mg twice daily. Her serum potassium is 2.9 mEq/L. She reports her legs feel heavy and weak. Respirations are 22 and shallow. The cardiac monitor shows prominent U waves. Lungs have fine crackles in the bases, unchanged from admission. Which finding requires the nurse's follow-up first?

options.text: Reports her legs feel heavy and weak
options.rationale: Skeletal muscle weakness. It can progress to flaccid paralysis, but the limbs are not the first threat to life.

options.text: Respirations 22 and shallow
options.rationale: The breathing muscles are weakening. This is the most dangerous finding on the list.

options.text: Cardiac monitor shows prominent U waves
options.rationale: The classic ECG sign of hypokalemia and a warning of dysrhythmias. It is a warning, while the shallow breathing is a failure already underway.

options.text: Lungs with fine crackles in the bases, unchanged from admission
options.rationale: Her heart failure baseline, not a potassium finding.

questions.takeaway: Low potassium weakens skeletal, respiratory and gut muscle. It also makes the heart prone to dysrhythmias. Check breathing before anything else.
questions.strategy: Every option is abnormal. The crackles are a trap because they involve the lungs. They belong to her heart failure and have not changed.

steps.detail: 2.9 with an active loop diuretic.
Unchanged crackles belong to heart failure.

steps.action: Rank the rest by the ABCs
steps.detail: Breathing muscle weakness comes before a rhythm warning or weak legs.

elimination.verdict: B. Shallow respirations mean the breathing muscles are failing.

questions.stem: A patient with a magnesium of 1.0 mEq/L is receiving IV magnesium sulfate. Which finding requires the nurse to stop the infusion and notify the provider?

options.text: Patellar reflexes 2+
options.rationale: Normal. Magnesium is not building up.

options.text: Absent patellar reflexes and respirations of 10
options.rationale: Magnesium toxicity. Reflexes disappear first, and breathing slows next. Stop the infusion; IV calcium is the antidote.

options.text: Blood pressure 118/74
options.rationale: Normal.

options.text: Reports feeling less shaky than this morning
options.rationale: The treatment is working.

questions.takeaway: During IV magnesium, check deep tendon reflexes. Lost reflexes and slow breathing mean the patient has swung from low magnesium to toxic levels.
questions.strategy: The patient started with low magnesium, so it is tempting to think only about hypomagnesemia. The danger during treatment is overcorrection.

steps.action: Think about the drug, not just the starting lab
steps.detail: IV magnesium can overshoot.
Deep tendon reflexes go first.
Respirations of 10 make it urgent.

elimination.verdict: Absent reflexes with respirations of 10.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old is brought from a care facility after three days of fever and poor oral intake. She is agitated and confused, with muscle twitching in her hands. Temperature 38.6 C, heart rate 108, blood pressure 104/62. Mucous membranes are dry. Serum sodium is 154 mEq/L. Which prescribed action addresses the cause of her findings?

options.text: Administer 3% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline raises sodium. It is for severe hyponatremia.

options.text: Restrict fluids to 1,000 mL per day
options.rationale: Restricting water makes a free water deficit worse. Fluid restriction treats the hyponatremia of SIADH.

options.text: Administer 0.45% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Fever, poor intake, dry mucosa and a sodium of 154 mean hypernatremia from free water loss. A hypotonic solution replaces free water, which is what she lost.

options.text: Assess for Chvostek sign and check the serum calcium
options.rationale: Twitching fits hypocalcemia. The sodium value and the story do not, so this chases the wrong electrolyte.

questions.takeaway: Hypernatremia in an older adult is usually water loss plus a thirst reflex that did not respond. Replace free water. Watch the sodium and the mental status as it comes down.
questions.strategy: 3% saline and fluid restriction are the hyponatremia treatments. They are offered to see whether you mix up the two directions.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Name the condition from the number and the story
steps.detail: Sodium 154 after fever and poor intake means she lost water.
3% saline and fluid restriction both push sodium the wrong way.
Twitching tempts you toward calcium. The sodium explains the whole picture.

steps.action: Pick the option that adds water
steps.detail: Hypotonic IV fluid replaces the free water she lost.

elimination.verdict: C. Hypernatremia from free water loss is treated with 0.45% sodium chloride.

questions.stem: A nurse receives report on four patients. Which patient does the nurse assess first?

options.text: Serum sodium 128 mEq/L, alert, reports a mild headache
options.rationale: Needs follow-up. She is alert, and a headache is an early finding.

options.text: Serum potassium 3.2 mEq/L, receiving oral potassium, reports leg cramps
options.rationale: The low potassium is being treated, and the symptom is expected.

options.text: Receiving IV magnesium sulfate, respirations 9, patellar reflexes absent
options.rationale: Magnesium toxicity during an infusion that is still running. Breathing is failing, so stop the infusion now.

options.text: Serum calcium 11.1 mg/dL, reports constipation
options.rationale: Slightly high with an expected symptom.

questions.takeaway: When four patients all have abnormal labs, choose the one whose airway or breathing is failing, and the one whose problem is still being made worse by something running.
questions.strategy: No lab value is given in option C. The respiratory rate is the value that matters.

steps.detail: Respirations of 9 in C.

steps.action: Ask whether the harm is ongoing
steps.detail: The infusion is still running.
Headache, cramps and constipation all match their labs and are stable.

elimination.verdict: The patient on IV magnesium with slow breathing and absent reflexes.

questions.stem: The nurse receives morning lab results for four patients. Which patient does the nurse see first?

options.text: Serum sodium 126 mEq/L, alert and oriented, reports a mild headache
options.rationale: Low and worth a call to the provider. She is alert, so the brain is coping for now, and a sodium this low usually got here over hours or days.

options.text: Blood glucose 30 mg/dL, diaphoretic and slow to answer questions
options.rationale: Brain cells run on glucose and have no reserve. A glucose of 30 with a neuro change can become a seizure or loss of consciousness within minutes, and the fix is fast and in your hands.

options.text: Serum potassium 3.4 mEq/L, reports feeling tired
options.rationale: Just below range with a vague symptom. Replace it, but it is not the emergency.

options.text: Serum sodium 147 mEq/L, reports thirst
options.rationale: Mildly high with the body's normal response. Encourage water and recheck.

questions.takeaway: The most abnormal number is not always the priority. Rank by how fast the problem can harm the patient and whether symptoms are already showing.
questions.strategy: Sodium 126 looks the most abnormal on paper. Glucose 30 with symptoms is the one that turns into a seizure before you finish rounds.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Look for symptoms, not just numbers
steps.detail: Two patients have symptoms: headache in A, sweating and slowed thinking in B. Slowed thinking is the brain sign.

steps.action: Ask how fast each one harms
steps.detail: Hypoglycemia injures the brain in minutes. Hyponatremia usually develops over hours or days.
Potassium 3.4 and sodium 147 are small deviations with expected symptoms.

elimination.verdict: The glucose of 30. Treat it now, then call about the sodium.

questions.stem: A nurse cares for a patient with a magnesium of 1.0 mEq/L and a patient with a magnesium of 4.0 mEq/L. Which assessment finding or history does the nurse associate with the patient whose magnesium is 4.0 mEq/L?

options.text: Hyperactive deep tendon reflexes and tremors
options.rationale: Nerves and muscles are overexcitable. That is low magnesium.

options.text: Diminished deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: Nerves and muscles are depressed. Reflexes fade as magnesium rises and can disappear at higher levels.

options.text: Seizures
options.rationale: The brain is overexcitable. That is low magnesium.

options.text: Chronic alcohol use with poor nutrition
options.rationale: Poor intake and losses through the kidneys and gut cause low magnesium.

questions.takeaway: Magnesium works like calcium. Low means excitable: brisk reflexes, tetany, seizures. High means sedated: no reflexes, slow heart, slow breathing.
questions.strategy: If you know calcium, you know magnesium. Both act as a brake on the nerves, so too much brake means everything slows. Three options describe the patient at 1.0 mEq/L.

steps.detail: Low means excitable; high means slow.
Brisk reflexes mean low magnesium; diminished reflexes mean high.
Alcohol use with poor nutrition loses magnesium. It belongs to the other patient.
Only one option shows a slowed nervous system.

elimination.verdict: B. Diminished deep tendon reflexes.

questions.stem: Which patient does the nurse see first?

options.text: Serum calcium 7.4 mg/dL, new hoarse voice and stridor
options.rationale: Laryngospasm from low calcium. The airway can close in minutes.

options.text: Serum calcium 10.9 mg/dL, reports constipation
options.rationale: Slightly high with an expected symptom. Stable.

options.text: Blood glucose 68 mg/dL, alert and eating lunch
options.rationale: Slightly low and she is already eating. Recheck in 15 minutes.

options.text: Serum sodium 134 mEq/L, reports mild fatigue
options.rationale: Barely low, with a vague symptom.

questions.takeaway: An abnormal lab with an airway finding comes before every other abnormal lab. Stridor is an airway emergency whatever the cause.
questions.strategy: Low glucose is a common first pick. This patient is alert and eating, so she is already fixing it herself.

steps.detail: Stridor is airway.

steps.action: Check whether each problem is already being handled
steps.detail: The low glucose patient is eating.
Calcium 10.9 and sodium 134 are close to normal.

elimination.verdict: Calcium 7.4 with stridor.

questions.stem: A patient with a potassium of 3.0 mEq/L has a prescription for IV potassium chloride. Which action by the nurse is appropriate?

options.text: Give the first 10 mEq by slow IV push to raise the level quickly
options.rationale: Never give potassium by IV push. A bolus can stop the heart.

options.text: Dilute the potassium in IV fluid and infuse it by pump at no more than 10 mEq per hour with the patient on a cardiac monitor
options.rationale: Potassium must be diluted. A pump keeps the rate controlled. The deck rate is 5 to 10 mEq per hour. Faster than that risks a dysrhythmia. The heart is what you are protecting while the level changes.

options.text: Give the dose intramuscularly if IV access is lost
options.rationale: Never give potassium IM or subcut. It causes severe tissue damage.

options.text: Check the IV site for burning or pain when the infusion is complete
options.rationale: Checking the site is correct. Waiting until the end is not. Potassium irritates veins, so check every hour. Burning can mean phlebitis or infiltration.

questions.takeaway: IV potassium: diluted, on a pump, no faster than 10 mEq per hour, site checked hourly, patient on a monitor. Never push, never IM.
questions.strategy: The word "slow" in the push option makes it sound safe. No IV push of potassium is safe. The site check is the right action at the wrong time.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Remove the two routes that are never allowed
steps.detail: IV push and IM.
"Slow" does not make a push safe.
A site check at the end of the infusion misses hourly irritation.

steps.action: Keep the option with every safeguard
steps.detail: Dilution, pump, rate limit and monitor.

elimination.verdict: B.

questions.stem: A patient with SIADH has a serum sodium of 124 mEq/L. His weight is up 2 kg. Crackles are heard in both lung bases. Which prescription does the nurse expect?

options.text: Restrict fluids
options.rationale: His sodium is low because of extra water, so you remove water rather than add salt. The cause and the fluid volume status decide the treatment. Low sodium from too much water needs fluid restriction.

options.text: Infuse 0.9% sodium chloride at 150 mL per hour
options.rationale: Adds volume to a patient who already has crackles. Saline is the fix for low sodium from losing sodium, not from too much water.

options.text: Encourage oral water intake
options.rationale: More water makes the sodium lower.

options.text: Give a potassium supplement
options.rationale: Does not address sodium or water.

questions.takeaway: Same sodium number, opposite fixes. Find the cause and volume status first. Then correct slowly so the brain can adjust.
questions.strategy: The crackles and weight gain decide it. He has too much water, so the right fix removes water.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weight gain and crackles mean excess.

steps.action: Match the fix to the cause
steps.detail: Remove water. Do not add sodium.
Saline and oral water both add fluid to an overloaded patient. Potassium does not touch the problem.

elimination.verdict: A. Restrict fluids.

questions.stem: A patient with a calcium of 7.2 mg/dL is twitching and reports painful hand cramps. The nurse places her in a quiet room to reduce stimulation. For acute tetany, which prescription does the nurse expect?

options.text: Oral calcium with the next meal
options.rationale: Too slow for tetany. Oral calcium is for mild or chronic cases. Vitamin D is added then because it helps the gut absorb calcium.

options.text: IV calcium
options.rationale: Severe or acute hypocalcemia needs IV replacement. Oral calcium is for mild or chronic cases.

options.text: IV furosemide
options.rationale: Furosemide increases calcium loss.

options.text: A calcitonin injection
options.rationale: Calcitonin lowers calcium.

questions.takeaway: For hypocalcemia, replace calcium: IV for tetany, oral for mild cases. Add vitamin D so it is absorbed. Reduce stimulation with a quiet room.
questions.strategy: Calcitonin and furosemide are hypercalcemia treatments. Check the direction before you pick a drug. Then let the word acute choose the route.

steps.detail: Calcitonin and furosemide lower calcium. She needs it raised.
Acute tetany needs the fastest route.

steps.action: Reject the right drug at the wrong time
steps.detail: Oral calcium fits mild or chronic cases, not tetany.

elimination.verdict: B. IV calcium.

questions.stem: A patient with kidney disease is receiving IV fluid with potassium added. The monitor shows tall peaked T waves and a widening QRS. The serum potassium is 6.9 mEq/L. The nurse has stopped the potassium infusion. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Give IV calcium as prescribed
options.rationale: Calcium protects the heart muscle within minutes. It does not lower the potassium; it buys time while the other drugs work.

options.text: Give regular insulin with dextrose as prescribed
options.rationale: Insulin moves potassium into cells. Dextrose prevents hypoglycemia. It is the right drug at the wrong time, because the ECG changes mean the heart needs protection first.

options.text: Give a potassium binder as prescribed
options.rationale: Removes potassium from the body through the GI tract. It is slower, so it comes after the heart is protected and the potassium is shifted.

options.text: Recheck the potassium and blood glucose
options.rationale: Rechecking confirms the level is falling and catches rebound low potassium or low glucose. It belongs at the end. The ECG changes already confirm the danger.

questions.takeaway: Stop, protect, shift, remove, recheck. Calcium comes before insulin because the heart is what kills.
questions.strategy: Students often pick insulin because it lowers the number. Calcium comes first because it protects the heart while the other drugs work.

steps.detail: The source is stopped. The key word is next.
Peaked T waves with a widening QRS mean the heart is at risk now. Calcium stabilizes it within minutes.
Insulin shifts, the binder removes, the recheck confirms. All three come after calcium.

elimination.verdict: A. Calcium protects the heart before anything lowers the level.

questions.stem: Eighteen hours after a total thyroidectomy, a patient reports tingling around her mouth and in her fingertips. Which finding requires the nurse's immediate action?

options.text: Positive Chvostek sign
options.rationale: Confirms low calcium, and it is a warning sign. It is not yet the airway.

options.text: High-pitched noisy breathing and a hoarse voice
options.rationale: Laryngospasm. Low calcium is making the larynx spasm, and the airway can close. Call for help and prepare IV calcium.

options.text: Muscle cramps in her calves
options.rationale: Expected in hypocalcemia and uncomfortable. Not an airway threat.

options.text: Incisional pain rated 5 out of 10
options.rationale: Expected after surgery. Treat it after the airway is safe.

questions.takeaway: After thyroid surgery, low calcium can close the airway. Stridor or a new hoarse voice outranks every other calcium finding.
questions.strategy: Chvostek sign is the answer students remember, which makes it the distractor. It confirms the problem; stridor is the emergency.

steps.detail: The parathyroid glands can be damaged during thyroid surgery.
Only one option is about breathing.
Chvostek sign and cramps confirm the problem; stridor is the danger.

elimination.verdict: Noisy high-pitched breathing. The airway comes first.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old taking hydrochlorothiazide has a serum sodium of 126 mEq/L. Which finding is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Reports mild nausea and a poor appetite
options.rationale: A real finding in hyponatremia, and it is uncomfortable rather than dangerous.

options.text: New confusion and difficulty staying awake since this morning
options.rationale: Cerebral change. Water is moving into brain cells inside a rigid skull, and confusion and lethargy are the steps before seizures and coma.

options.text: Urine output of 40 mL per hour
options.rationale: Adequate output. Nothing to act on.

options.text: Dry oral mucous membranes
options.rationale: Points to volume status, which matters for choosing treatment. It does not threaten her the way the brain change does.

questions.takeaway: In sodium imbalance, the brain is the organ at risk. A change in level of consciousness is the finding you act on first.
questions.strategy: Every option could appear in a patient with low sodium. Ask which one belongs to the organ that cannot swell safely.

steps.detail: Sodium moves water into and out of brain cells.
40 mL per hour is fine.
Nausea and dry mucosa are uncomfortable. New confusion is progressing.

elimination.verdict: New confusion and lethargy. Protect the brain first.

questions.stem: A nurse compares two patients. One has a potassium of 2.8 mEq/L. The other has a potassium of 6.2 mEq/L. Which finding does the nurse associate with the patient whose potassium is 2.8 mEq/L?

options.text: Tall peaked T waves with a widened QRS
options.rationale: The classic high potassium ECG. It belongs to the patient whose potassium is 6.2.

options.text: Hyperactive bowel sounds with abdominal cramping
options.rationale: The gut is irritable in high potassium. Diarrhea can cause low potassium, but hyperactive cramping is a finding of the high level.

options.text: Flat T waves with prominent U waves
options.rationale: The classic low potassium ECG. Low potassium slows things down.

options.text: Taking spironolactone and an ACE inhibitor
options.rationale: Both drugs keep potassium in the body. They point to hyperkalemia.

questions.takeaway: Low potassium slows things: flat T, U wave, sluggish gut. High potassium irritates things: peaked T, diarrhea. Loop diuretics lower potassium; spironolactone and ACE inhibitors raise it.
questions.strategy: Every wrong option is true for the other patient. Sort each one into low or high before you choose. Slow and flat means low. Peaked, fast and potassium sparing means high.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Flat T with U wave is low. Peaked T is high.
Hyperactive cramping is fast, so it belongs to the high level.
Spironolactone and ACE inhibitors keep potassium. They belong to the high patient.

elimination.verdict: C is the only option that fits a potassium of 2.8.

questions.stem: A patient with lung cancer has a serum calcium of 13.1 mg/dL. Which prescription does the nurse anticipate implementing first to lower the calcium?

options.text: IV 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Normal saline helps the kidneys excrete calcium and corrects the dehydration that often comes with it.

options.text: IV furosemide started right away
options.rationale: A loop diuretic increases calcium excretion. It is given once fluid volume is restored, because diuresing a dry patient worsens the dehydration.

options.text: A bisphosphonate as prescribed
options.rationale: It keeps calcium in the bone instead of the blood. It is part of the plan but does not come before hydration.

options.text: Hold oral calcium supplements
options.rationale: Stop every source of calcium. Holding a supplement does not remove the calcium already in the blood.

questions.takeaway: For hypercalcemia: flush with normal saline first, then add a loop diuretic once volume is restored. Stop the sources, keep calcium in the bone and put the patient on a monitor.
questions.strategy: All four options belong in the plan. The question is order. Furosemide is the correct drug at the wrong time if the patient is still dry.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what each option does to calcium
steps.detail: All four help lower it or keep it from rising.
Hydration comes before diuresis.
Holding a supplement and a bisphosphonate do not clear the calcium already in the blood.

elimination.verdict: A. Normal saline comes first.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic alcohol use is admitted with a magnesium of 1.1 mEq/L. Which finding does the nurse expect?

options.text: Absent deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: That is high magnesium.

options.text: Respiratory depression
options.rationale: High magnesium depresses breathing. Low magnesium does not.

options.text: Hyperactive deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: Low magnesium makes nerves excitable, the same as low calcium. Brisk reflexes are the deck's key sign of low magnesium.

options.text: Flushing and a feeling of warmth
options.rationale: Flushing comes from the vasodilation of high magnesium.

questions.takeaway: Low magnesium looks like low calcium: Chvostek sign, brisk reflexes, tetany, prolonged QT. It also travels with low potassium and low calcium, so replace magnesium to fix them.
questions.strategy: Three options belong to high magnesium. Decide the direction first, then pick the finding that matches.

steps.detail: 1.1 is low. Low magnesium means excitable.
Absent reflexes, slowed breathing and flushing all belong to high magnesium.
Hyperactive reflexes are the odd one out and the answer.

elimination.verdict: C. Low magnesium gives brisk reflexes.

questions.stem: A nurse is assigned four patients. Which patient does the nurse assess first?

options.text: Serum potassium 6.4 mEq/L, heart rate 48, tall peaked T waves on the monitor
options.rationale: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes and bradycardia means the heart is already affected. The next rhythm may be ventricular fibrillation.

options.text: Serum potassium 3.3 mEq/L, reports leg cramps, taking oral potassium with breakfast
options.rationale: Low, treated, and the symptom is expected. Stable.

options.text: Serum sodium 133 mEq/L, alert, eating breakfast
options.rationale: Just below range with no symptoms.

options.text: Serum potassium 5.3 mEq/L, normal sinus rhythm, no complaints
options.rationale: Mildly high with a normal rhythm. Recheck it and review medications, but the heart is not affected yet.

questions.takeaway: In hyperkalemia, ECG changes mean the heart is already involved. A high potassium with peaked T waves and bradycardia beats every other abnormal lab on the floor.
questions.strategy: Two patients have high potassium. The ECG tells you which one is unstable.

steps.detail: Only option A has rhythm changes.

steps.action: Compare the two high potassium patients
steps.detail: 5.3 with a normal rhythm is stable. 6.4 with peaked T waves is not.
Cramps with a low potassium that is being replaced are expected.

elimination.verdict: Potassium 6.4 with peaked T waves and bradycardia.

questions.stem: A nurse cares for two patients. The first has a serum osmolarity of 312 mOsm/L, which is above the normal range of 270 to 300 mOsm/L. The provider orders 0.45% sodium chloride. The nurse expects it to move water into the shrunken cells. The second patient has new swelling of the brain. The provider orders the same fluid for this patient. The nurse questions the second order. Which rationale supports the nurse's decision?

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride contains too much sodium
options.rationale: It contains half the sodium of plasma.

options.text: Hypotonic fluid expands plasma volume too quickly
options.rationale: Most of it leaves the vessels. The danger is where the water goes, not how fast the plasma grows.

options.text: A hypotonic fluid moves water into brain cells and can worsen the swelling
options.rationale: The brain sits in a rigid skull with little room to swell. Adding free water to swollen cells raises intracranial pressure.

options.text: Only colloids can be given to patients with neurologic problems
options.rationale: An absolute that is not true. Isotonic crystalloids are commonly used.

questions.takeaway: Water follows solute. Hypotonic fluid swells cells, hypertonic fluid shrinks them. Colloids hold water in the vessels by oncotic pressure.
questions.strategy: For each fluid, ask where the water will end up. Then ask whether that place needs water or is already swollen. The same movement that helps the first patient harms the second.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 0.45% sodium chloride is hypotonic. It has half the sodium of plasma, so A is false.
Hypotonic fluid leaves the vessels and moves into cells. B worries about the wrong compartment.
"Only colloids" is not true for neurologic patients.
Free water into swollen brain cells raises intracranial pressure.

elimination.verdict: C. Hypotonic fluid worsens brain swelling.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old is on postoperative day 1 after a hip repair. She has received lactated Ringer's at 125 mL per hour plus two 500 mL boluses for low urine output overnight. Weight is 64.3 kg, up from 62.1 kg before surgery. Vital signs at 0400 were BP 132/78, HR 84, RR 18, SpO2 96% on room air. At 0800 they are BP 158/90, HR 96 and bounding, RR 26, SpO2 91% on room air. Neck veins are distended with the head of the bed at 45 degrees. Fine crackles are heard in both lung bases. Urine output was 30 mL per hour for the last 2 hours. Hematocrit is 31%, down from 36% before surgery. Serum sodium is 133 mEq/L. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Give another 500 mL bolus because urine output is only 30 mL per hour
options.rationale: This is the order that caused the problem. 30 mL/hr is at the usual minimum. Her rising BP, bounding pulse, neck vein distention and crackles show overload. More fluid pushes her toward pulmonary edema.

options.text: Slow the infusion to the lowest prescribed rate and notify the provider
options.rationale: She has fluid volume excess. She is receiving more fluid than her heart and kidneys can handle. You stop adding to the problem first, then get a prescription such as a loop diuretic.

options.text: Recheck lung sounds, respiratory rate and SpO2 in 1 hour to confirm the trend
options.rationale: Monitoring the lungs is correct because worsening crackles and falling saturation show pulmonary edema progressing. The trend is already confirmed over 4 hours. Waiting another hour while the fluid runs lets her get worse.

options.text: Weigh her daily on the same scale, at the same time, in the same clothing
options.rationale: The deck calls rapid weight gain the best indicator of fluid overload. One liter of fluid weighs about 1 kg. Daily weight tracks her response over days. It does nothing for her lungs this morning.

questions.takeaway: In an older adult receiving IV fluid, rising weight, bounding pulse, distended neck veins and new crackles mean overload. Stop adding fluid first. Then sit her up and watch the lungs.
questions.strategy: Two findings (low urine output and a falling hematocrit) look like bleeding. Read the whole trend. Rising BP with bounding pulse and neck vein distention cannot be hypovolemia. Her hematocrit is low because the blood is diluted.

steps.action: Name the problem from the trend
steps.detail: BP, HR and RR all rose over 4 hours while SpO2 fell. Weight is up 2.2 kg. This is fluid volume excess.
A diluted hematocrit falls in overload too. Bleeding would flatten the neck veins and weaken the pulse.
The bolus makes pulmonary edema worse.
Rechecking in an hour and a daily weight are monitoring. The data already calls for action. Stopping the source comes first.

elimination.verdict: B.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing how hormones regulate fluid output in several patients on a medical unit. Which situation describes a response caused primarily by aldosterone?

options.text: A patient has gone 14 hours without water. Serum osmolarity is 308 mOsm/L. Urine becomes small in volume and dark.
options.rationale: High osmolarity triggers ADH from the posterior pituitary. The kidneys reabsorb water, so urine becomes concentrated.

options.text: A patient with heart failure has atrial stretch from fluid overload. The body responds by excreting sodium and water.
