questions.stem: A patient has been immobile in bed for two weeks following a spinal cord injury. The nurse finds that both feet rest with the toes pointed downward and the ankles can no longer be brought to a neutral position. Which complication has developed?

options.text: Bone demineralization
options.rationale: Bone demineralization is the loss of mineral from bone that is not being loaded. It shows on imaging or in calcium studies, not as a joint that will not move.

options.text: Foot drop, which is a plantar flexion contracture
options.rationale: A contracture is the permanent shortening of muscle and tendon that limits joint mobility, and plantar flexion is the toes-pointed position of the ankle. That is foot drop, and it is prevented by maintaining neutral alignment, performing range of motion, and using supportive devices.

options.text: Muscle atrophy
options.rationale: Atrophy is the shrinking of muscle that is not being used. This patient almost certainly has atrophy too, and atrophy does not lock a joint in a fixed position, which is what the stem describes.

options.text: Venous stasis
options.rationale: Venous stasis is blood pooling in the legs because the muscle pump has stopped working. It raises the risk of thrombus formation and presents as swelling or as a clot, not as a rigid ankle.

questions.takeaway: Contractures are permanent shortening, so prevention is the whole intervention. Range of motion, neutral alignment, and supportive devices are scheduled rather than offered when there is time.

questions.stem: A patient is on bed rest after spinal surgery. The nurse hears diminished breath sounds at both lung bases with no adventitious sounds, notes that the patient's cough is weak, and finds that the oxygen saturation has fallen from 97 to 92 percent. The temperature is 36.8 C. Which complication is developing?

options.text: Pneumonia
options.rationale: Pneumonia is infection of the lung tissue. It has not yet.

options.text: Thrombus formation in the legs
options.rationale: A thrombus is a clot forming in a vein where blood has stopped moving. Thrombus is a genuine risk for this patient and is not what these findings describe.

options.text: Atelectasis
options.rationale: Atelectasis is the collapse of small airways and alveoli that are not being inflated. Diminished sounds without adventitious sounds means air is not reaching the area rather than moving through something.

options.text: Negative nitrogen balance
options.rationale: Negative nitrogen balance means the body is breaking down more protein than it takes in. It is a metabolic effect of immobility, not a respiratory one.

questions.takeaway: Flat positioning reduces lung expansion, a weak cough leaves secretions in place, and the dependent bases collapse first. Atelectasis is the step before pneumonia, not the same thing.

questions.stem: A patient has been on prolonged bed rest. For each nursing action, indicate the complication of immobility it is intended to prevent.

rows.text: Sits the patient upright and has the patient cough and deep breathe every two hours
rows.rationale: Atelectasis is the collapse of alveoli that are not being inflated. Lung expansion and the movement of retained secretions, which are the two things that fail when a patient stays flat.

rows.text: Applies sequential compression devices and has the patient perform leg exercises
rows.rationale: Venous stasis is blood pooling in the legs once the muscle pump stops working. Movement of blood out of the legs, which is what prevents a clot from forming.

rows.text: Takes every joint through its full arc twice daily
rows.rationale: A contracture is permanent shortening of muscle and tendon that limits joint mobility. Range of motion is the direct prevention.

rows.text: Repositions the patient on a schedule and lifts rather than drags during the move
rows.rationale: Pressure, friction, and shear are the three mechanical forces that injure skin, and all three reduce circulation to the tissue. The schedule limits time under pressure, and lifting instead of dragging removes friction and shear.

rows.text: Raises the head of the bed in stages and has the patient sit at the edge of the bed before standing
rows.rationale: Orthostatic hypotension is a fall in blood pressure when the patient moves upright, so the brain briefly goes short. Time for the circulation to adjust before the patient takes weight, which is why gradual position changes are the listed prevention.

rows.text: Positions a supportive device against the soles of the feet to hold the ankles in neutral alignment
rows.rationale: Foot drop is a plantar flexion contracture, the ankle setting with the toes pointed. This is the second action in the set aimed at contracture, because two different measures prevent the same complication.

questions.takeaway: Immobility damages seven systems through three mechanisms: stasis of fluids, pressure on tissue, and disuse of muscle, bone, and joint. Name the mechanism and the matching intervention follows.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A patient reports knee pain and instability after a twisting injury. The knee is swollen and the patient cannot fully straighten it.

The study that will show whether a bone is broken is [[1]].

The imaging is clear, but the pain and the instability continue. The study best able to show a torn ligament is [[2]].

A fracture is still suspected even though the imaging looked normal. The study that may reveal it is [[3]].

options.text: an x-ray
options.rationale: An x-ray passes radiation through tissue and shows dense structures clearly. It is the first study for a possible broken bone because it answers that question quickly.

options.text: a computed tomography scan
options.rationale: Computed tomography builds cross-sectional images and gives more detail of bone than a plain film. It earns its place with complex fractures, once a fracture is known or strongly suspected.

options.text: an ultrasound
options.rationale: Ultrasound uses sound waves and can assess tendons, muscles, fluid collections, and some joint abnormalities. Bone reflects the sound, so it is not the study for a suspected fracture.

options.text: magnetic resonance imaging
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging shows soft tissue best. This is the right study for a different question in the same knee.

options.text: a computed tomography scan
options.rationale: Computed tomography is the detailed bone study. This is the near miss, because both this and the correct answer are cross-sectional and both sound like more information than an x-ray.

options.text: a bone scan
options.rationale: A bone scan detects areas of increased bone activity, such as occult fractures, infection, or tumors. A ligament tear does not light up a bone scan.

options.text: magnetic resonance imaging
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is best for soft tissue, including muscles, ligaments, tendons, cartilage, spinal structures, and bone marrow. Persistent instability with clear plain imaging points at ligament rather than bone.

options.text: a dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry scan
options.rationale: This scan measures bone mineral density and is used to assess osteoporosis. It answers a question about how strong bone is over time, not what tore today.

options.text: a bone scan
options.rationale: A bone scan detects areas of increased bone activity, and healing or injured bone is metabolically active. Occult means present but not visible on ordinary imaging, which is exactly the situation in this sentence.

options.text: a dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry scan
options.rationale: This scan measures bone mineral density. It reports how dense the bone is, which is a different question from whether this bone is cracked.

options.text: a computed tomography scan
options.rationale: Computed tomography provides more detailed bone images and is useful for complex fractures. This is the strongest distractor, because more detail sounds like the way to find something that is hiding.

options.text: an ultrasound
options.rationale: Ultrasound assesses tendons, muscles, fluid collections, and some joint abnormalities. No, sound does not penetrate bone well enough to answer that.

questions.takeaway: Match the study to the tissue and to the question. X-ray for a suspected break, computed tomography for detail on bone, magnetic resonance imaging for soft tissue, bone scan for a fracture nothing else has shown, and dual-energy absorptiometry for density.

questions.stem: A patient has 5 of 5 muscle strength in both legs but sways and grabs the bedrail when standing with eyes closed. Which system is most likely impaired?

options.text: Skeletal muscle strength
options.rationale: Already measured as full. Strength is not the failing component.

options.text: Joint range of motion
options.rationale: Limits how far a joint moves. It does not produce instability at rest in standing.

options.text: Bone density
options.rationale: Affects fracture risk, not postural control.

options.text: Proprioception and balance
options.rationale: Proprioception is awareness of body position without looking. Losing vision removes the backup, so the sway appears.

questions.takeaway: Strength and balance fail separately. A strong patient can still be unsafe to walk.

questions.stem: Which outcome does proper body alignment produce?

options.text: Reduced stress on joints and less fatigue
options.rationale: Alignment lets bone carry weight through bone. Poor alignment makes muscle hold the load, and muscle tires.

options.text: Increased muscle bulk
options.rationale: Bulk comes from loading the muscle, not from posture.

options.text: Faster wound healing
options.rationale: Unrelated to the mechanical effects of alignment.

options.text: Improved appetite
options.rationale: Not among the outcomes of alignment.

questions.takeaway: Alignment promotes efficient movement, minimizes joint stress, reduces fatigue, and improves balance.

questions.stem: During the Bedside Mobility Assessment Tool, a patient cannot sit at the side of the bed unassisted and is unable to reach across midline. Which level applies?

options.text: Level 2, maximum assist
options.rationale: Assigned when a patient sits successfully but cannot extend the leg and point the toes.

options.text: Level 1, total assist
options.rationale: Failing the sit and shake test means trunk strength and seated balance are inadequate. The assessment stops here.

options.text: Level 3, moderate assist
options.rationale: Assigned when a patient cannot lift the buttocks off the bed. This patient never reached that test.

options.text: Level 4, minimum assist
options.rationale: Requires advancing a step, which is three tests away.

questions.takeaway: You stop at the first test the patient cannot complete, and that failure names the level.

questions.stem: A patient is unconscious after a traumatic brain injury and cannot initiate any movement. Which exercise maintains joint flexibility?

options.text: Active range of motion
options.rationale: Requires the patient to move the joint. This patient cannot initiate movement.

options.text: Active-assistive range of motion
options.rationale: Requires the patient to start the movement so the nurse can complete it.

options.text: Passive range of motion
options.rationale: The nurse moves the joint entirely. It maintains flexibility and prevents contractures when the patient can contribute nothing.

options.text: Isometric exercise
options.rationale: Requires voluntary muscle contraction.

questions.takeaway: Passive is correct only when the patient cannot contribute. It maintains flexibility and builds no strength.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews musculoskeletal changes with an older adult. Which finding is not an expected change with aging?

options.text: Muscle tissue atrophy
options.rationale: Expected. Muscle mass declines with age, contributing to weakness and slowed movement.

options.text: Decreased range of motion
options.rationale: Expected. Cartilage becomes less elastic and compressible, so joints move through a smaller arc.

options.text: Increased cartilage elasticity
options.rationale: The change runs the other way. Cartilage becomes less elastic.

options.text: Osteopenia or osteoporosis
options.rationale: Expected. Bone density falls, which is why height loss and fracture risk rise.

questions.takeaway: Expected aging changes are not the same as disease. They still raise injury risk. Muscle, bone and cartilage all lose something with age.
questions.strategy: The stem asks for what is not expected. Every aging change in this system is a loss, so the one option describing a gain is the answer.

steps.detail: "Not an expected change" means pick the false statement.
Atrophy, less motion and less bone density are all losses.
Increased elasticity is the only gain.

elimination.verdict: C.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a casted arm and cannot palpate the radial pulse. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Document the finding and recheck in one hour
options.rationale: Delays confirmation of whether blood is reaching the hand.

options.text: Elevate the arm above the level of the heart
options.rationale: Raising a limb that may already be underperfused reduces arterial inflow further.

options.text: Apply warm compresses to improve circulation
options.rationale: Does not address a possible obstruction and delays the assessment.

options.text: Use a Doppler to check for flow, then compare with the other arm
options.rationale: A Doppler detects flow that cannot be felt. Comparing sides turns an uncertain finding into a clear one.

questions.takeaway: Absent or diminished pulses is a red flag. Confirm with Doppler and always compare sides.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease wants to begin an exercise program. Which modification does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Shorter sessions paced to the patient's tolerance with rest periods
options.rationale: Activity plans are modified rather than cancelled in chronic illness, and tolerance sets the pace.

options.text: Avoid all physical activity to conserve oxygen
options.rationale: Inactivity worsens deconditioning and breathlessness over time.

options.text: High-intensity intervals to build endurance quickly
options.rationale: Exceeds tolerance and risks severe dyspnea.

options.text: Exercise only while receiving nebulizer treatments
options.rationale: Not a standard modification and unnecessarily restricts when the patient can move.

questions.takeaway: Activity plans are modified in coronary artery disease, hypertension, COPD, diabetes, and immobility.

questions.stem: Which question best establishes a patient's mobility baseline on admission?

options.text: Are you afraid of falling here?
options.rationale: Assesses fear, which is worth knowing and is not a baseline of function.

options.text: Do you use any assistive devices at home?
options.rationale: Identifies what the patient normally relies on, which defines the starting point for the plan.

options.text: Would you like help getting up?
options.rationale: Offers assistance before any assessment has been done.

options.text: Has anyone in your family had a hip fracture?
options.rationale: Family history contributes nothing to this patient's current function.

questions.takeaway: Start every mobility assessment at baseline, then look for what is new.

questions.stem: A patient three days past abdominal surgery tolerates sitting upright at the edge of the mattress for several minutes and shakes hands firmly. With both feet flat on the floor and the knees below hip level, the patient cannot extend either leg or flex the ankles. The patient insists on standing. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Allow a standing attempt with one person assisting, since sitting balance is intact
options.rationale: Sitting balance was demonstrated and leg strength was not. Standing is the next test, and this patient did not clear the one before it.

options.text: Document moderate assist and attempt a stand with a gait belt
options.rationale: Moderate assist is assigned when a patient cannot lift the buttocks off the bed. The assessment stopped before that test, so this level was never demonstrated.

options.text: Document maximum assist and use a device or additional staff for any transfer
options.rationale: Failing the stretch and point test means lower-extremity strength is inadequate to progress toward standing. The patient's willingness does not change the finding, and the level determines the equipment used.

options.text: Repeat the sitting portion of the assessment before proceeding
options.rationale: Sitting was already passed. Repeating a cleared test delays the transfer without adding information.

questions.takeaway: The tool stops at the first failure, and that failure sets the equipment. A patient's readiness to try is not a level.

questions.stem: During a mobility assessment a patient stands, holds the position, marches in place, and advances each foot forward and back. While doing so the patient repeatedly lets go of the walker to gesture and states there is no need for it. Which nursing action follows?

options.text: Document the patient as independent and remove the walker from the room
options.rationale: Physical performance was adequate and safety awareness was not. Removing the device acts on half the assessment.

options.text: Assign a lower mobility level because the walker was released
options.rationale: The level is set by what the patient can physically do. Letting go of the device is a safety finding to address, not a downgrade of demonstrated strength.

options.text: Restrict the patient to bed until a physical therapy evaluation is completed
options.rationale: Restriction produces the weakness the assessment exists to prevent, and the patient has just demonstrated the ability to step.

options.text: Ambulate with standby assistance and address the safety awareness before independence
options.rationale: Advancing a step meets the criterion for the highest level, and that level is assessed together with balance, stability, gait, and safety awareness. Strength is demonstrated and judgment is not, so supervision continues.

questions.takeaway: The walk test scores balance, stability, gait, and safety awareness. A strong patient with poor judgment is not independent.

questions.stem: A nurse tests upper extremity strength. The right arm lifts off the bed and holds against moderate downward pressure before giving way. The left arm lifts off the bed but drops as soon as any pressure is applied. How does the nurse document this?

options.text: Right 4 of 5, left 3 of 5
options.rationale: Movement against some resistance is grade 4, and movement against gravity alone with no resistance tolerated is grade 3. Both cleared gravity, which puts both above grade 2.

options.text: Right 5 of 5, left 4 of 5
options.rationale: Full strength holds against firm resistance without giving way, and the right arm gave way under moderate pressure.

options.text: Right 4 of 5, left 2 of 5
options.rationale: Grade 2 is movement only when gravity is removed. The left arm lifted off the bed, so it cleared gravity.

options.text: Right 3 of 5, left 2 of 5
options.rationale: Understates both. Tolerating moderate resistance is above grade 3, and lifting against gravity is above grade 2.

questions.takeaway: Grade 3 is the gravity hinge. Below it the limb only moves in a supported plane, above it you are adding resistance.

questions.stem: Six hours after a below-knee cast was applied for a fibular fracture, a patient has pain rated 9 of 10 that increased after the last analgesic dose. The toes are swollen and cool, capillary refill is 5 seconds, and the patient reports the foot feels numb. The opposite foot is warm with refill under 2 seconds. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Elevate the extremity above heart level to reduce the swelling
options.rationale: Elevation reduces swelling in a limb with intact perfusion. Raising a limb that is already underperfused lowers arterial inflow further.

options.text: Notify the provider immediately and keep the limb at heart level
options.rationale: Pain disproportionate to the injury and unrelieved by analgesia, with delayed refill, coolness, and new numbness on one side, is compromised perfusion. Keeping the limb level preserves arterial inflow while help is summoned.

options.text: Administer the next dose of analgesia and reassess in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Analgesia has already failed, which is data rather than a reason to repeat it. Thirty minutes is time the limb does not have.

options.text: Apply ice over the cast and document the neurovascular findings
options.rationale: Cold causes vasoconstriction in a limb with failing circulation, and documenting is not an intervention.

questions.takeaway: Pain out of proportion and unrelieved by opioids in a casted limb is a circulation problem until proven otherwise. Always compare sides.

questions.stem: A patient in the clinic has lost 5 cm of height over eight years, fractured a wrist catching a fall from standing, and reports mid-back pain that began without injury. Which diagnostic study does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the thoracic spine
options.rationale: Best for soft tissue such as ligaments, cartilage, cord, and marrow. It will not answer whether bone density is low.

options.text: Computed tomography of the wrist
options.rationale: Gives detailed bone images for mapping a complex fracture. The fracture is already known and is not the underlying question.

options.text: Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry
options.rationale: Height loss, a fracture from a low-energy fall, and atraumatic back pain together point to reduced bone density. This scan measures bone mineral density and is the study used to assess osteoporosis.

options.text: A bone scan
options.rationale: Detects increased bone activity such as an occult fracture, infection, or tumor. It does not measure how dense the bone is.

questions.takeaway: Read the findings as a group. Height loss plus a fragility fracture plus atraumatic pain is a density question, not an imaging-the-injury question.

questions.stem: A patient with several weeks of progressive proximal muscle weakness has a creatine kinase of 4200 units/L, an elevated aldolase, and an elevated aspartate aminotransferase. The alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin are normal. What do these results support?

options.text: Hepatic injury
options.rationale: Aspartate aminotransferase is found in both liver and muscle, which is why the stem includes the other liver studies. Normal alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin make a liver source unlikely.

options.text: Reduced bone mineral density
options.rationale: Measured by a density scan. These are muscle enzymes and say nothing about bone.

options.text: An inflammatory joint process
options.rationale: Assessed by imaging and joint fluid analysis. Weakness described as proximal and enzymes from muscle point away from the joints.

options.text: Muscle tissue damage
options.rationale: These enzymes are released from injured muscle cells. Normal alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin argue against a liver source for the elevated aminotransferase, which leaves muscle.

questions.takeaway: Creatine kinase, aldolase, lactate dehydrogenase, and aspartate aminotransferase rise with muscle damage. The other liver values are what separate muscle from liver.

questions.stem: A patient of 62 with a family history of osteoporosis asks how to protect bone and muscle over the coming years. Which statement by the patient indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will walk on most days of the week."
options.rationale: Correct understanding. Loading bone is what keeps mineral in it. Loading muscle is what maintains strength. Both are named among the measures that promote musculoskeletal health.

options.text: "I will make sure I get enough calcium and vitamin D."
options.rationale: Correct understanding. Appropriate intake is listed among the measures that maintain bone over time.

options.text: "I will stop smoking."
options.rationale: Correct understanding. Avoiding tobacco is named directly among the measures that promote musculoskeletal health.

options.text: "I will switch from walking to swimming to spare my joints."
options.rationale: Needs further teaching. Swimming is good conditioning but removes the weight bearing that maintains bone density. It supplements rather than replaces.

questions.takeaway: Activity, weight bearing, calcium with vitamin D, no tobacco, limited alcohol. Non-weight-bearing exercise does not protect bone.
questions.strategy: The stem asks for the wrong statement. Swimming sounds healthy, which is exactly why it works as the trap.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Find the statement that would not protect bone.
Bone keeps mineral only when it bears weight.
D replaces weight bearing with a non-weight-bearing activity.

elimination.verdict: D. Swimming does not load bone.

questions.stem: Two patients are assessed on the same morning. Patient one has 5 of 5 strength in all extremities and full range of motion but cannot rise from a chair without using both armrests and stops twice crossing the room. Patient two has 4 of 5 strength and mildly reduced shoulder range but dresses, transfers, and walks the hallway without stopping. Which statement about their functional ability is accurate?

options.text: Patient two has the higher functional ability, because functional ability is measured by tasks accomplished
options.rationale: Functional ability is what the patient can do: turn, sit unsupported, stand, transfer, walk, and perform activities of daily living. Strength and range are components, and neither predicts performance on its own.

options.text: Patient one has the higher functional ability, because strength and range of motion are normal
options.rationale: Those are two measurements taken at rest. This patient cannot rise unaided or cross a room without stopping, which is what function measures.

options.text: The two patients have equivalent functional ability
options.rationale: One completes daily tasks without stopping and the other cannot. The difference is exactly what a functional assessment captures.

options.text: Functional ability cannot be compared without a formal strength grade for both
options.rationale: Both strength grades are given, and function is assessed by observing tasks rather than by grading muscles.

questions.takeaway: Strength is a number at rest. Function is what the patient accomplishes, and the two come apart in real patients.

questions.stem: A nurse in a senior health clinic assesses several adults over 75 years of age. Which findings require follow-up? Select all that apply.

options.text: Walks more slowly than a year ago with a steady, even gait
options.rationale: Movement slows with age. The gait is steady and symmetric, so it is expected.

options.text: Shoulder range of motion slightly reduced on both sides with no pain
options.rationale: Cartilage becomes less elastic and ROM decreases. Symmetry and no pain keep it in the expected range.

options.text: Right knee hot, red and swollen since yesterday
options.rationale: A sudden, one-sided inflammatory joint is not aging. Infection or gout has to be ruled out.

options.text: Thigh muscles visibly smaller on both sides with strength 4 of 5
options.rationale: Muscle tissue atrophies with age. Equal loss with good strength fits.

options.text: Lost 4 cm of height with new mid-back pain that began without injury
options.rationale: Pain with no injury plus height loss suggests a vertebral compression fracture from osteoporosis.

options.text: Left calf 3 cm larger than the right after a week of limited activity
options.rationale: One-sided calf swelling after reduced activity is a clot until proven otherwise.

questions.takeaway: Aging changes are gradual, symmetric and painless. Sudden onset, one side only, heat or pain without injury moves a finding out of the expected group.
questions.strategy: Look at three features in each option: speed of onset, symmetry and pain. Any one that is abnormal is enough to require follow-up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Both sides equal points to aging. One knee or one calf does not.
Since yesterday or new pain points to a problem.
Painless decline is expected. New back pain without injury is not.

elimination.verdict: Follow up on the hot knee, the height loss with back pain and the larger left calf.

questions.stem: A patient has been on bed rest for five days after a pelvic fracture and now has a prescription to ambulate with a walker as tolerated. The patient is oriented and eager to walk. The nurse measures blood pressure and pulse with the patient lying down. The nurse then raises the head of the bed in stages and helps the patient sit at the edge of the bed. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Have the patient straighten each knee and point the toes
options.rationale: Tests leg strength and stability before you ask the legs to hold body weight. It comes after sitting tolerance is confirmed.

options.text: Recheck blood pressure and pulse after one minute of sitting and confirm the patient can sit unsupported and reach across midline
options.rationale: Checks for orthostatic hypotension and sitting balance at once. If either fails you stop here.

options.text: Have the patient rise and hold the buttocks off the bed for a count of five
options.rationale: Tests whether the legs can support a stand. Standing before the sitting recheck risks a fall from orthostatic hypotension.

options.text: Have the patient march in place, then walk with the walker
options.rationale: Stepping is tested before walking. It is the last stage, not the next one.

questions.takeaway: Get up in stages and test each stage before the next. Baseline, dangle and recheck, then legs, then stand, then step.
questions.strategy: The eager patient invites you to skip ahead. Each step answers a question the next step depends on.

steps.detail: Baseline taken and already sitting.

steps.action: Ask what the sit just changed
steps.detail: Blood pressure after five days of bed rest.
Sit, legs, stand, step.

elimination.verdict: B. Recheck vitals and sitting balance before the legs take weight.

questions.stem: Day 10: 84-year-old admitted after a left-sided stroke, mostly in bed since admission. Expressive aphasia unchanged since admission. Right arm strength 2 of 5, unchanged. Right ankle rests at 10 degrees of plantar flexion and cannot be dorsiflexed to neutral; was neutral on admission. No bowel movement in 4 days; abdomen distended. Urine cloudy with a strong odor. Diminished breath sounds in both bases; oxygen saturation 97% on day 8, 95% on day 9, 93% today. Nonblanchable redness over the sacrum. Heart rate 76, blood pressure 134/80 lying. Passed swallow screen; eating 75% of meals. Which complication of immobility is the nurse's priority to address?

options.text: Nonblanchable redness over the sacrum
options.rationale: Pressure over a bony area without repositioning is an early pressure injury. It is a real complication, but it does not threaten gas exchange.

options.text: Diminished breath sounds in both bases with oxygen saturation falling from 97% to 93%
options.rationale: A steady decline with reduced basal sounds suggests atelectasis from poor lung expansion. Each value alone looks acceptable. The trend does not. Breathing comes first.

options.text: No bowel movement in 4 days with a distended abdomen
options.rationale: Immobility slows GI motility and causes constipation. It needs treatment, after breathing.

options.text: Right ankle fixed at 10 degrees of plantar flexion
options.rationale: A new loss of dorsiflexion is an early plantar flexion contracture, which leads to foot drop. It develops over days and is not the immediate threat.

questions.takeaway: Immobility reaches nearly every system. When several complications are present, the ABCs decide which comes first. Read the oxygen trend rather than one value.
questions.strategy: Every option is a true complication of immobility. The saturation of 93% looks acceptable on its own, which is the trap; the falling trend with diminished bases is a breathing problem.

steps.action: Confirm all four are immobility complications
steps.detail: Skin, bowel and ankle are all real. None is wrong, so priority decides.
97 to 95 to 93 is a decline.
A breathing problem outranks skin, bowel and joint problems.

elimination.verdict: B. Declining oxygenation with diminished bases.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old is on day 4 after a bowel resection. Yesterday's Bedside Mobility Assessment Tool (BMAT) result was Level 2. This morning the patient is oriented x4 with no signs of delirium. The patient sits unassisted at the side of the bed for three minutes, reaches across midline and shakes the nurse's hand. With both feet on the floor the patient straightens each knee and points the toes. Asked to rise, the patient lifts the buttocks off the bed but sits back down at a count of two with both legs trembling. Heart rate 84 before and 96 after the attempt, returning to 86 within two minutes. Oxygen saturation 95% throughout. No dizziness. Which action is most appropriate for moving the patient from the bed to the chair?

options.text: Walk the patient to the chair with a gait belt and one person
options.rationale: Walking belongs to Level 4. The patient could not hold a stand for a count of five.

options.text: Use a full-body mechanical lift for the transfer
options.rationale: Safe, but too restrictive. It removes the weight bearing the patient can do and slows progress.

options.text: Keep the patient in bed until the stand can be held for a count of five
options.rationale: Bed rest deepens the weakness that caused the failed stand.

options.text: Use a sit-to-stand lift for the transfer
options.rationale: The patient passed sit and shake and stretch and point but could not hold the stand, which is Level 3. Partial leg strength needs equipment that lets the patient bear some weight while the device supports the rest.

questions.takeaway: The BMAT level is the first test the patient fails. It picks the equipment. The plan should use every bit of strength the patient has.
questions.strategy: Two options are safe but wrong. The full lift under-uses the patient and bed rest reverses progress. Pick the option that matches the level exactly.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The stand, held only to two. That is Level 3, not yesterday's Level 2.
Walking with one person requires passing the stand.
A full-body lift and bed rest both waste the strength the patient has.
Level 3 means a sit-to-stand aid.

elimination.verdict: D. Use a sit-to-stand lift.

questions.stem: Which assessment question best evaluates a patient's memory?

options.text: Count backward from 100 by 7s.
options.rationale: Serial 7s test attention and calculation, not memory.

options.text: Explain the meaning of a common fable.
options.rationale: Interpreting a fable tests abstract thinking.

options.text: Describe how you came to the hospital.
options.rationale: Recalling a recent event tests memory directly.

options.text: Copy a word onto paper.
options.rationale: Copying tests motor function and following directions.

questions.takeaway: Memory is tested by asking the patient to recall something that happened. Serial 7s test attention; fables test abstract thinking.
questions.strategy: Match each option to the brain function it actually tests, then pick the one that matches the stem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A is attention, B is abstract reasoning, D is motor and following directions.
Only C asks the patient to pull up a recent event from memory.

elimination.verdict: C is the only option that makes the patient remember something.

questions.stem: An older adult patient who was oriented this morning suddenly becomes confused. What should the nurse assess first?

options.text: SpO2
options.rationale: Hypoxia is a fast, reversible cause of acute confusion and falls under breathing in the ABCs.

options.text: Temperature
options.rationale: Infection can cause confusion, but oxygenation is the more immediate threat.

options.text: Medication reconciliation
options.rationale: Important later, but it takes time and does not address an immediate threat.

options.text: Electrolytes
options.rationale: Needs a lab draw and results; check oxygenation first.

questions.takeaway: A sudden change in mental status is a new cue that needs action now. Oxygenation is checked first because hypoxia is quick to find and quick to fix.
questions.strategy: When every option is a possible cause, use the ABCs to choose which one to check first.

steps.detail: Hypoxia, infection, medications, and electrolytes can all cause confusion.
Oxygenation is breathing, so it comes before the other causes.
SpO2 takes seconds at the bedside. Labs and a medication review take longer.

elimination.verdict: SpO2 is the priority because it is an ABC finding and the fastest to correct.

questions.stem: A patient with a frontal lobe injury is admitted to the unit. Which intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Enable the bed alarm.
options.rationale: The frontal lobe controls judgment and impulse control. Poor judgment raises fall risk, and a bed alarm protects the patient without relying on judgment.

options.text: Use a picture board for communication.
options.rationale: Picture boards help with aphasia, which is more closely tied to language areas.

options.text: Place all items directly in front of the patient.
options.rationale: This helps with visual field loss or neglect, not frontal lobe deficits.

options.text: Teach the patient to use the call light before getting up.
options.rationale: This depends on judgment and memory, the very functions a frontal lobe injury impairs.

questions.takeaway: Frontal lobe damage impairs judgment and impulse control. Choose safety measures that do not depend on the patient remembering or deciding to follow them.
questions.strategy: Link the brain region to its function, then ask which intervention still works if that function is lost.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It handles judgment, impulse control, personality, and planning.
B is for aphasia, C is for visual field loss or neglect.
D sounds good, but it asks an impaired patient to use judgment.

elimination.verdict: The bed alarm is correct because it keeps the patient safe without depending on judgment.

questions.stem: A patient opens the eyes when spoken to, gives confused answers, and follows commands. What is the Glasgow Coma Scale score?

options.rationale: This undercounts one of the components.
This undercounts one of the components.
Eyes to voice = 3, confused = 4, obeys commands = 6. Total 13.
This would need spontaneous eye opening (4) or oriented speech (5).

questions.takeaway: GCS: eyes 4, verbal 5, motor 6. Score each part separately, then add. The range is 3 to 15.
questions.strategy: Write out E, V, and M before looking at the options so the distractors cannot anchor you.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Opens to voice = 3.
Confused = 4.
Obeys commands = 6.

elimination.verdict: 13 is correct.

questions.stem: A patient opens the eyes only to a painful stimulus, makes moaning sounds without words, and pulls the hand away from the painful stimulus. What is the GCS score?

options.rationale: Too low. Recheck the motor score.
Too low. Withdrawal is 4, not 3.
Eyes to pain = 2, sounds = 2, withdraws = 4. Total 8.
Too high. Moaning is sounds (2), not words (3).

questions.takeaway: A GCS of 8 or less signals severe impairment and a patient who may not protect the airway.
questions.strategy: Separate withdrawal (4, pulls away) from abnormal flexion (3, decorticate), and sounds (2) from words (3).

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: To pain = 2.
Moaning with no words = sounds = 2.
Pulls away from pain = withdraws = 4.

elimination.verdict: 8 is correct. The traps are scoring moaning as words or withdrawal as flexion.

questions.stem: The nurse finds a patient with arms extended at the sides, wrists turned outward, and feet pointed down. What does this finding indicate?

options.text: Decorticate posturing from damage above the brainstem
options.rationale: Decorticate arms flex inward toward the core.

options.text: Decerebrate posturing from brainstem involvement
options.rationale: Extension posturing points to the brainstem and is the more severe of the two.

options.text: An expected response to pain in a sedated patient
options.rationale: Both postures are always abnormal.

options.text: Localizing to pain, a purposeful movement
options.rationale: Localizing means reaching toward the stimulus.

questions.takeaway: Decorticate: flexion, arms toward the core, damage above the brainstem. Decerebrate: extension, arms away, brainstem, more severe. Both need immediate action.
questions.strategy: Use the memory hook: deCORticate = toward the CORe (flexion). Extension points to decerebrate.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Extended arms and pointed feet are extension, so decerebrate.
Posturing is never normal, even with sedation.
Localizing is purposeful reaching, scored 5.

elimination.verdict: Decerebrate posturing from the brainstem is correct.

questions.stem: A patient can name objects correctly and understands questions, but the words come out slurred. How should the nurse describe this problem?

options.text: A language problem, which is a cognitive function
options.rationale: The patient understands and finds the right words, so language is intact.

options.text: A speech problem, which is a motor function
options.rationale: Speech is the physical production of words. Right words, poor production = speech (motor) problem.

options.text: A problem with orientation
options.rationale: Orientation is knowing person, place, time, and situation.

options.text: A problem with level of consciousness
options.rationale: LOC is how awake the patient is.

questions.takeaway: Language is understanding and choosing words (cognitive). Speech is producing them (motor). New changes in either may signal neurologic dysfunction.
questions.strategy: Ask: are the words right? If yes and they sound wrong, it is speech.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The patient understands, so receptive language is intact.
The patient names objects correctly, so expressive language is intact.
Slurring is a motor problem with making the sounds.

elimination.verdict: Speech (motor) is correct.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old patient's daughter says, "Mom has been a little forgetful for years, but today she can't find her words and her right hand is weak. I guess it's just her age." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Slower thinking and some memory changes are expected at her age."
options.rationale: True of gradual changes, but it dismisses a sudden new deficit.

options.text: "These are sudden changes, so I'm going to assess her right now."
options.rationale: Sudden or new neurologic changes are never assumed to be aging. Assess immediately.

options.text: "Let's watch her for a few hours and see if it gets better."
options.rationale: Waiting delays care for a possible stroke.

options.text: "I'll ask the provider to order a memory test tomorrow."
options.rationale: Delays assessment of an acute change.

questions.takeaway: Aging slows processing, reflexes, and pupil response gradually. Sudden or one-sided changes are never aging and need immediate assessment.
questions.strategy: Separate gradual from sudden. The word "today" and a one-sided finding make this acute.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Word-finding trouble and right hand weakness started today.
A is technically true about aging but ignores the new deficit.
C and D postpone assessment.

elimination.verdict: B is correct because a new neurologic change means assess now.

questions.stem: The nurse is performing a cranial nerve assessment on a patient who is NPO for surgery. Which action is appropriate?

options.text: Give a sip of water to test swallowing.
options.rationale: Never test swallowing with fluids when the patient is NPO.

options.text: Skip the swallow test and assess facial symmetry and pupils.
options.rationale: Swallowing is observed only if clinically appropriate. Other cranial nerve checks, including the gag reflex, still apply.

options.text: Give ice chips instead of water to test swallowing.
options.rationale: Ice chips are still something by mouth.

options.text: Postpone the entire neurologic assessment until after surgery.
options.rationale: Only the swallow part is deferred.

questions.takeaway: Do not test swallowing with fluids or ice chips if the patient is NPO. The gag reflex and the rest of the cranial nerves are still assessed as usual.
questions.strategy: Watch for options that quietly break an order, like ice chips for an NPO patient.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Give nothing by mouth when NPO. CN IX and X can still be checked with the gag reflex and uvula rise.
Ice chips still go by mouth.
D skips the whole assessment when only one part is off limits.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: Which pupil documentation is most accurate?

options.text: Pupils normal.
options.rationale: Too vague to compare to later checks.

options.text: Pupils 3 mm, equal, round, brisk reaction to light bilaterally.
options.rationale: Size in millimeters, equality, shape, and reaction can be trended.

options.text: Pupils medium size and reactive.
options.rationale: Size must be measured in millimeters.

options.text: PERRLA.
options.rationale: Acceptable shorthand in some settings, but gives no size to compare to baseline.

questions.takeaway: Document pupil size in millimeters (normal 2 to 6 mm), equality, shape, and speed of reaction. Change from baseline matters most.
questions.strategy: Pick the documentation someone else could use to spot a change.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Size in mm, equal, round, brisk, sluggish, or nonreactive.
"Normal" and "medium" can't be trended.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A student asks how the body knows a hand touched a hot stove and pulls away. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Efferent nerves carry the heat sensation to the brain, and afferent nerves move the hand.
options.rationale: The directions are reversed.

options.text: Afferent nerves carry the sensation toward the CNS, and efferent nerves carry the signal to the muscles.
options.rationale: Afferent = arrives at the CNS. Efferent = exits to muscles and organs.

options.text: The autonomic nervous system handles both the sensation and the movement.
options.rationale: Skeletal muscle movement is not autonomic.

options.text: Cranial nerves carry the signal from the hand.
options.rationale: Spinal nerves serve the limbs.

questions.takeaway: Afferent pathways carry signals toward the CNS. Efferent pathways carry signals away from the CNS to muscles and organs.
questions.strategy: Afferent Arrives. Efferent Exits.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sensation arrives (afferent). Movement exits (efferent).
C is autonomic; D is cranial nerves, which serve the head.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A frightened patient has a heart rate of 118 and dilated pupils. Which part of the nervous system is responsible?

options.text: Parasympathetic
options.rationale: Rest and digest slows the heart and constricts the pupils.

options.text: Sympathetic
options.rationale: Fight or flight raises heart rate, dilates pupils, and mobilizes energy.

options.text: Cerebellum
options.rationale: Controls balance and coordination.

options.text: Somatic motor nerves
options.rationale: Control voluntary skeletal muscle.

questions.takeaway: Sympathetic = fight or flight: faster heart, dilated pupils. Parasympathetic = rest and digest: slower heart, digestion.
questions.strategy: Link the finding to fight or flight versus rest and digest.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fear, tachycardia, dilated pupils.
All three are fight or flight.

elimination.verdict: Sympathetic is correct.

questions.stem: The provider orders a test to evaluate a patient's brain electrical activity after a possible seizure. Which test does the nurse expect?

options.text: EMG
options.rationale: EMG evaluates nerve and muscle disorders.

options.text: EEG
options.rationale: EEG records brain electrical activity.

options.text: Lumbar puncture
options.rationale: Assesses cerebrospinal fluid.

options.text: Transcranial Doppler
options.rationale: Measures cerebral blood flow.

questions.takeaway: EEG = brain electrical activity. EMG = nerves and muscles. MRI = soft tissue. CT = structure. LP = CSF. Transcranial Doppler = blood flow.
questions.strategy: E for electrical, E for encephalo (brain): EEG. M for muscle: EMG.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Brain electrical activity.
EMG looks similar but is muscle.

elimination.verdict: EEG is correct.

questions.stem: A patient admitted for pneumonia had a normal neurologic exam on admission. Today the nurse notices a new tremor in the left hand. What type of assessment is appropriate now?

options.text: Comprehensive neurologic assessment
options.rationale: Used for new admissions or a broad baseline.

options.text: Focused neurologic assessment
options.rationale: Targeted assessment is performed when a change from baseline is noted.

options.text: No assessment; document the tremor only
options.rationale: A new finding needs assessment.

options.text: Psychosocial assessment
options.rationale: Does not evaluate the new motor finding.

questions.takeaway: Comprehensive = broad baseline for new admissions or neurologic concerns. Focused = targeted when a change from baseline is noted or to monitor a known problem.
questions.strategy: Ask what triggered the assessment: a new admission or a new change.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A change from an established baseline.
Changes from baseline call for a focused assessment.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: To assess cranial nerve VII, the nurse asks the patient to do which of the following?

options.text: Follow a finger with the eyes.
options.rationale: Eye movements are CN III, IV, and VI.

options.text: Smile, raise the eyebrows, and show the teeth.
options.rationale: CN VII (facial) controls facial movement. Look for drooping or asymmetry.

options.text: Swallow a sip of water.
options.rationale: Swallowing is CN IX and X.

options.text: Shrug the shoulders.
options.rationale: Shoulder shrug is CN XI.

questions.takeaway: CN VII: smile, raise eyebrows, show teeth, compare both sides. CN IX and X: swallowing, only if appropriate.
questions.strategy: Picture what the nerve moves.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Facial nerve, facial expression.
Eyes (III, IV, VI), swallow (IX, X), shrug (XI).

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A patient who was alert this morning is now suddenly confused. Which possible causes should the nurse consider? Select all that apply.

options.text: Low oxygen level
options.rationale: Hypoxia is a fast, reversible cause.

options.text: Low or high blood glucose
options.rationale: Glucose problems commonly cause acute confusion.

options.text: Infection
options.rationale: Infection, including UTI or sepsis, can cause acute confusion, especially in older adults.

options.text: A new medication
options.rationale: Sedatives, opioids, and anticholinergics are common causes.

options.text: Electrolyte imbalance
options.rationale: Sodium imbalance in particular affects the brain.

options.text: Normal aging
options.rationale: Aging is gradual. A sudden change is never assumed to be aging.

questions.takeaway: For a sudden mental status change, think oxygenation, glucose, infection, medications, electrolytes, and other acute causes. Never blame aging.
questions.strategy: Every true acute cause is correct. Remove only the option that explains away the change.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Oxygenation, glucose, infection, medications, electrolytes, acute causes.
Aging is gradual. "Sudden" rules it out.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are correct.

questions.stem: The nurse assesses an 82-year-old patient. Which finding requires immediate follow-up?

options.text: Slower reaction time
options.rationale: Processing speed and reaction time slow with age.

options.text: Diminished deep tendon reflexes
options.rationale: Expected with aging.

options.text: New weakness of the left arm
options.rationale: One-sided weakness is not aging. Assess immediately.

options.text: Decreased sensitivity to touch and temperature
options.rationale: Expected. It is a burn and injury risk to teach about.

questions.takeaway: Aging slows things down evenly and gradually. New, sudden, or one-sided changes are not aging.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding by speed of onset and symmetry.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reaction time, reflexes and sensation are expected with aging.
New arm weakness needs action.

elimination.verdict: C. New one-sided weakness is never aging.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing several older adult patients. For each finding, indicate whether it is an expected age-related change or requires immediate follow-up.

rows.text: Takes longer to answer questions but answers correctly
rows.rationale: Slower processing with correct answers is expected.

rows.text: Right facial droop noticed during lunch
rows.rationale: New facial asymmetry suggests a stroke.

rows.text: Wakes several times during the night
rows.rationale: Altered sleep and more nighttime waking are expected.

rows.text: Left pupil 6 mm and sluggish; right pupil 3 mm and brisk
rows.rationale: Unequal pupils with a sluggish reaction can signal rising ICP.

rows.text: Diminished ankle reflexes on both sides
rows.rationale: Diminished reflexes on both sides are expected.

rows.text: Garbled speech that started an hour ago
rows.rationale: New speech changes may signal neurologic dysfunction.

questions.takeaway: Expected aging changes are gradual and symmetric. New, sudden, or one-sided findings need immediate assessment.
questions.strategy: For each row, ask: is it new, sudden, or one-sided? If yes, it needs follow-up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rows 2 and 6 describe a recent onset.
Row 4 compares unequal pupils.

steps.action: Keep bilateral, gradual changes as expected
steps.detail: Rows 1, 3, and 5.

elimination.verdict: Expected: 1, 3, 5. Follow-up: 2, 4, 6.

questions.stem: A patient was alert and oriented 30 minutes ago. The nurse now notices new confusion, slurred speech, and right-sided weakness. The nurse recognizes this as a change from baseline. Following the class sequence for a new neurologic change, which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Notify the provider or activate the stroke alert
options.rationale: New confusion, slurred speech, and one-sided weakness within 30 minutes suggest a stroke. Escalation is needed, but it is the last step of the class sequence so the call includes the data the team needs.

options.text: Assess the patient immediately
options.rationale: Step 2 on the class slide. A new neurologic change means act now. Acting starts with assessing the patient in front of you.

options.text: Compare the findings to the prior baseline
options.rationale: Step 3. You need current findings before you have anything to compare.

options.text: Reorient the patient and recheck in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Waiting treats a sudden change as minor. A new neurologic change is never watched and rechecked later.

questions.takeaway: A new neurologic change means act now: recognize, assess, compare, ABCs and vitals, notify. This is the order on your class slide. On the NCLEX, if the patient looks unstable, the ABCs come first.
questions.strategy: Assessment comes before notification, so the call includes the data the team needs. Watch the word "next": recognition is already done.

steps.detail: Reorienting and rechecking later delays care for a possible stroke.
You cannot compare findings you have not gathered. The call comes after assessment.
Assess the patient immediately.

elimination.verdict: B. Assess the patient immediately.

questions.stem: A nurse is using the Glasgow Coma Scale to monitor a patient's level of consciousness. Which statement about the GCS is accurate?

options.text: Scores range from 0 to 15
options.rationale: Each component scores at least 1, so the total can never be 0. The lowest possible score is 3, deep coma.

options.text: Pupil response is one of the three scored components
options.rationale: Pupils are checked in every neuro assessment. They are not part of the GCS score. The three components are eye opening, verbal response and motor response.

options.text: The most important information comes from the trend over time
options.rationale: A falling trend signals deterioration and needs action now.

options.text: The verbal score alone gives the most useful information
options.rationale: Verbal is one of three components. Intubated or aphasic patients cannot be scored on it fairly.

questions.takeaway: GCS = eyes (4), verbal (5), motor (6). Range 3 to 15. Watch the trend; a falling score means act now.
questions.strategy: Remember the maximums 4, 5, 6 and the minimum of 1 each. One score is a snapshot and hides direction.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Eyes, verbal, motor. Pupils are checked but are not part of the GCS.
Verbal alone cannot be scored fairly in intubated or aphasic patients.

elimination.verdict: C.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews this note on a patient. 0800: alert and oriented to person, place, time and situation. 1100: opens eyes only when name is called loudly. Hand grips equal and strong. Right pupil 5 mm, sluggish; left pupil 3 mm, brisk. Reports mild hunger. Answers are confused; unable to state the year. Which set of findings requires immediate follow-up?

options.text: Opens eyes only to a loud voice, unequal pupils with a sluggish right pupil, confused answers
options.rationale: Each is a decline from the 0800 baseline. LOC has dropped from alert to opening eyes only to a loud voice. Unequal pupils with a sluggish reaction are a change that needs action. New confusion is a change from baseline.

options.text: Equal strong grips, mild hunger, confused answers
options.rationale: Confusion needs follow-up. Equal strong grips and mild hunger are not neurologic declines.

options.text: Opens eyes only to a loud voice, equal strong grips, unequal pupils
options.rationale: The eye opening and the pupils need follow-up. Equal strong grips are a stable finding.

options.text: Alert and oriented at 0800, mild hunger, unequal pupils
options.rationale: The pupils need follow-up. The 0800 finding is the baseline. Hunger is not a neurologic decline.

questions.takeaway: Compare every finding to baseline. A decline in LOC, new confusion or unequal pupils means assess and report now.
questions.strategy: Read the baseline first. An option is right only if every finding in it changed for the worse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 0800: fully alert and oriented.
Eye opening, pupils, orientation.

steps.action: Drop any set with a stable finding
steps.detail: Equal grips, hunger and the baseline itself knock out B, C and D.

elimination.verdict: A. All three findings are declines.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a new graduate about the Glasgow Coma Scale. Which statement by the new graduate requires further teaching?

options.text: "A GCS of 15 means the patient is fully alert."
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: "A drop from 14 to 11 needs immediate action."
options.rationale: Correct. A declining score signals deterioration.

options.text: "A single score tells me more than the trend."
options.rationale: Incorrect. The trend over time is what matters most.

options.text: "The lowest possible score is 3."
options.rationale: Correct.

questions.takeaway: One GCS score is a snapshot. The trend shows whether the patient is getting better or worse.
questions.strategy: In "requires further teaching" items, look for the one false statement.

steps.detail: 15 = alert, decline = act, lowest = 3.
The slide says trend over time is critical.

elimination.verdict: C requires further teaching.

questions.stem: A patient on a neurologic unit is unresponsive to voice. Yesterday, when the nurse applied a trapezius squeeze, his arms bent tightly toward the chest with wrists and fingers curled in and his legs extended. Today the same stimulus produces arms that are rigidly extended and rotated, legs extended and feet pointed down. Which interpretation by the nurse is correct?

options.text: He has changed from decerebrate to decorticate posturing, which shows the injury is improving
options.rationale: The names are reversed. Flexion toward the core is decorticate and extension away from the body is decerebrate. Moving from flexion to extension is a decline.

options.text: He has changed from decorticate to decerebrate posturing, which shows the injury now involves the brainstem and is worsening
options.rationale: Flexion toward the core is decorticate, motor 3. Extension away from the body is decerebrate, motor 2. The slides call decerebrate the more severe sign. A change from decorticate to decerebrate means the patient is getting worse.

options.text: Both responses are withdrawal from pain, a normal response that scores motor 4
options.rationale: Withdrawal is normal flexion away from the stimulus. It changes with where the pain is. Posturing looks the same no matter where the pain is, so neither response is withdrawal.

options.text: Both responses show damage above the brainstem with the brainstem still working
options.rationale: True of decorticate posturing only. Decerebrate posturing means the brainstem is involved.

questions.takeaway: Decorticate is flexion to the core, above the brainstem, motor 3. Decerebrate is extension, brainstem, motor 2 and worse. Withdrawal and localizing are normal responses.
questions.strategy: Name each posture by direction first. Flexion to the core is decorticate. Extension away is decerebrate. Then decide whether the change is better or worse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Withdrawal and localizing respond to where the pain is. Neither posture does, so C is out.
Yesterday was flexion, which is decorticate. Today is extension, which is decerebrate.
A and B are an opposite pair. Decerebrate involves the brainstem and is worse, so D is only half true.

elimination.verdict: Decorticate to decerebrate, a worsening injury that now involves the brainstem.

questions.scenario: A 71-year-old was admitted for observation after a fall at home. He takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. At 1600 he was alert and oriented x4 with a GCS of E4 V5 M6. Pupils were 3 mm, equal and brisk. At 1900 the nurse finds him asleep. He opens his eyes when his name is spoken and says he is "at the store." He squeezes and releases the nurse's hand on command. The right pupil is 4 mm and sluggish and the left is 3 mm and brisk. BP 146/88 (148/86 at 1600), HR 76, RR 16, SpO2 96%. His wife says, "He is always tired by evening."
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the patient is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Check airway, breathing and vital signs at the bedside
options.rationale: A falling LOC can compromise the airway. You confirm ABCs before anything else.

options.text: Notify the provider immediately using the 1600 findings as the comparison
options.rationale: The slides say a declining score requires immediate action. Giving the baseline makes the change clear.

options.text: Let him sleep and repeat the GCS at the next scheduled check
options.rationale: The correct step at the wrong time. Waiting until the next scheduled check on a patient taking warfarin with a new pupil change can cost brain tissue.

options.text: Reorient him and dim the lights for evening confusion
options.rationale: Accepts the wife's explanation. He was oriented three hours ago, so this is a new change, not a pattern.

options.text: Declining level of consciousness indicating neurologic deterioration
options.rationale: GCS fell from 15 to 13 (E3 V4 M6) and one pupil became larger and sluggish. Both are changes from his own baseline.

options.text: Normal evening fatigue
options.rationale: Fatigue does not make a person disoriented or change one pupil.

options.text: Stable status because the GCS is still above 8
options.rationale: True that 13 is not a coma score. The trend is what matters. A drop of 2 in three hours is significant.

options.text: Decerebrate posturing
options.rationale: He obeys commands, which scores motor 6. Posturing would score 2 or 3.

options.text: GCS with each component recorded
options.rationale: Recording E, V and M shows exactly which response is changing and lets everyone compare the same way.

options.text: Pupil size in millimeters and reaction to light
options.rationale: An oval or sluggish pupil that is growing is an early warning of pressure on CN III. Millimeters let you compare with the last check.

options.text: Orientation to time only
options.rationale: Too narrow. It misses eye opening, motor response and pupils.

options.text: Temperature every 4 hours
options.rationale: Useful in general care, but it does not track the problem he has now.

questions.takeaway: A drop in GCS from the patient's own baseline is a new cue that needs action now, even when the number still looks acceptable.
questions.strategy: The wife's comment and the stable vital signs invite you to wait. LOC changes first. Vital sign changes come late, after the brainstem is compressed.

steps.detail: Eyes to voice 3, confused 4, obeys 6. Total 13, down from 15.
New disorientation and a new unequal, sluggish pupil.

steps.action: Reject the explanations that delay care
steps.detail: Evening fatigue and a score above 8 do not explain a change.
ABCs, notify, then GCS components and pupils.

elimination.verdict: Neurologic deterioration; check ABCs and notify now; track GCS components and pupils in mm.

questions.stem: A nurse is performing a focused motor and sensory assessment on an alert 66-year-old with type 2 diabetes who reports new numbness in the left hand. Which action reflects correct technique?

options.text: Test only the left hand, since that is where the symptom is
options.rationale: Without the right side you have nothing to compare. You could miss a wider pattern.

options.text: Begin with nail bed pressure to confirm he responds to pain
options.rationale: He is alert and talking. A painful stimulus is used only when LOC is decreased.

options.text: Record the numbness as expected with aging because he is over 65
options.rationale: Aging lowers sensation gradually and on both sides. New numbness on one side is never assumed to be aging.

options.text: With his eyes closed, touch matching spots on both sides and ask, "Does this feel the same on both sides?"
options.rationale: The slides say to always compare right and left. The patient's own side is the best control. Closing his eyes tests sensation, not vision.

questions.takeaway: Motor and sensory checks are comparisons. Test both sides, remove visual cues. Never file a new one-sided change under aging.
questions.strategy: His diabetes offers an easy explanation for the numbness. That is true, but it is not a reason to skip the comparison or to call it age-related.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Right and left, with visual cues removed.

steps.action: Match the stimulus to the LOC
steps.detail: He is alert, so no pain stimulus.
Aging is gradual and on both sides. Testing only the left removes the control.

elimination.verdict: D, the bilateral comparison with eyes closed.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses three patients on a neurologic unit. Patient 1 names every object correctly and follows commands, but his words are slurred. Patient 2 speaks fluently in full sentences that make no sense and cannot follow the command "squeeze my hand." Patient 3 has a new right facial droop when asked to smile and show her teeth. It is time for her scheduled oral medications. Which action by the nurse is the priority?

options.text: Document that patient 1 has a change in speech, a motor function
options.rationale: Accurate. He has the right words and the problem is producing them. It is a documentation task, not the priority.

options.text: Confirm that patient 2 can hear and is being spoken to in his primary language before documenting a language deficit
options.rationale: Accurate. A language barrier or hearing loss can mimic a comprehension problem. It takes seconds, but no airway is at risk.

options.text: Call the rapid response team for patient 2
options.rationale: If this is a new change it is urgent. But you must first know the finding is real, which means ruling out hearing and language barriers.

options.text: Hold patient 3's oral medications, keep her NPO until her swallowing is evaluated and notify the provider of the new droop
options.rationale: Facial weakness from CN VII can come with weakness of the swallowing muscles (CN IX and X). A new droop is also an acute neurologic change the provider needs now. Protect the airway and report. The medication schedule waits.

questions.takeaway: Slurred with the right words is speech. Wrong words or poor understanding is language. Rule out hearing and language barriers first. Protect the airway and report a new facial droop before giving pills.
questions.strategy: Two options are true statements that carry no immediate risk. One is the right escalation before the finding is confirmed. Only patient 3 has an airway at stake.

steps.detail: Ask who is in danger right now.
Patient 2 needs hearing and language checked before a rapid response call.
New facial weakness means NPO until swallowing is evaluated.

elimination.verdict: D. Hold oral meds, keep NPO and notify for patient 3.

questions.stem: A stroke alert is called for a patient with sudden left arm weakness. What information matters most to the stroke team right now?

options.text: The patient's favorite food
options.rationale: Not relevant to emergency care.

options.text: The time the patient was last known well
options.rationale: Last known well starts the treatment clock and decides whether a clot buster is possible.

options.text: The number of people in the family
options.rationale: Not relevant to emergency care.

options.text: The patient's seasonal allergies
options.rationale: Allergies matter for drugs, but they do not decide treatment eligibility.

questions.takeaway: Time is brain. Last known well decides whether the patient can receive a fibrinolytic or clot removal.
questions.strategy: Ask which piece of history is time sensitive.

steps.detail: A and C have no bearing on stroke care.
Allergies matter, but LKW decides eligibility.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old patient has trouble finding words, right-sided weakness, and has been incontinent of urine. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Provide perineal care.
options.rationale: Important for skin, but not the priority.

options.text: Assess the gag reflex.
options.rationale: Any stroke can cause dysphagia. Aspiration threatens the airway.

options.text: Elevate the head of the bed to 30 degrees.
options.rationale: A good supportive action, but it does not assess the threat.

options.text: Change the bed linens.
options.rationale: Comfort and skin care come later.

questions.takeaway: Airway comes first. Check swallowing and gag before anything else; the visible problem is often a distractor.
questions.strategy: Ignore the most visible problem and look for the ABC threat.

steps.detail: Incontinence is visible, but it is not life threatening.
Stroke can cause dysphagia and aspiration.
C is an intervention; B assesses the actual risk.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A patient admitted yesterday with a stroke asks for breakfast. Which task can the RN delegate to assistive personnel?

options.text: Perform the bedside swallow screen.
options.rationale: Swallow assessment is an RN responsibility.

options.text: Feed the patient after the RN confirms the swallow screen was passed.
options.rationale: Feeding can be delegated once swallowing is confirmed safe.

options.text: Give the patient sips of water to see how well she swallows.
options.rationale: This is a swallow assessment.

options.text: Feed the patient now because she is hungry.
options.rationale: Feeding before a swallow screen risks aspiration.

questions.takeaway: The RN does the swallow screen. Assistive personnel can feed only after the screen is passed.
questions.strategy: Assessment stays with the RN. Look for the option that keeps it there.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A and C are both swallow assessments.
D skips the screen.
B has the RN confirming first.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A patient is 24 hours after an ischemic stroke. Which finding is the earliest sign of increased intracranial pressure?

options.text: Fixed, dilated pupils
options.rationale: A late sign.

options.text: Restlessness and new confusion
options.rationale: Declining LOC, including restlessness and confusion, is the earliest sign.

options.text: Bradycardia with widened pulse pressure
options.rationale: Part of the Cushing triad, a late sign.

options.text: Decerebrate posturing
options.rationale: A late sign.

questions.takeaway: The earliest sign of increased ICP is a change in LOC. Fixed pupils, posturing, and the Cushing triad are late.
questions.strategy: "Earliest" means pick the subtlest change, not the most dramatic.

steps.detail: Pupils, posturing, and Cushing triad are late.
Restlessness and confusion show a change in LOC.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A patient with increased ICP becomes less responsive. Which vital sign pattern should the nurse recognize as the Cushing triad?

options.text: Hypotension, tachycardia, rapid shallow breathing
options.rationale: This pattern suggests shock.

options.text: Hypertension with widened pulse pressure, bradycardia, irregular breathing
options.rationale: The brainstem's late response to high ICP.

options.text: Hypertension, tachycardia, fever
options.rationale: Not the Cushing pattern.

options.text: Hypotension, bradycardia, warm dry skin
options.rationale: Suggests neurogenic shock.

questions.takeaway: Cushing triad: rising BP with widening pulse pressure, falling heart rate, irregular breathing. A very late sign; act immediately.
questions.strategy: BP goes up while the heart rate goes down. That opposite movement is the clue.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hypotension points to shock, not ICP.
High BP, low HR, irregular breathing.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for a patient with increased ICP who needs a bath, linen change, suctioning, and repositioning. What is the best plan?

options.text: Do all of the care at once so the patient can rest afterward.
options.rationale: Back-to-back care can spike ICP.

options.text: Space the care out with rest periods between activities.
options.rationale: Clustering raises ICP. Spacing care keeps pressure down.

options.text: Keep the head of the bed flat during care.
options.rationale: HOB up per protocol, often 30 degrees, helps venous drainage.

options.text: Suction every hour to keep the airway clear.
options.rationale: Suction only when needed; suctioning raises ICP.

questions.takeaway: With high ICP you space out care. This is the opposite of the usual rule to cluster care.
questions.strategy: Watch for a usually correct rule that flips for this patient.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clustering is usually right, but not with high ICP.
Flat HOB and routine suctioning raise ICP.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A patient with type 1 diabetes arrives with slurred speech and confusion. Blood glucose is 52 mg/dL. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Prepare the patient for a fibrinolytic.
options.rationale: Symptoms may be from hypoglycemia, not stroke.

options.text: Treat the hypoglycemia per protocol, then reassess the neurologic status.
options.rationale: Hypoglycemia mimics stroke. Correct it and recheck.

options.text: Complete the NIHSS before treating the glucose.
options.rationale: Delays a quick, reversible fix.

options.text: Give a regular meal tray.
options.rationale: Swallowing is not confirmed, and the glucose needs faster treatment.

questions.takeaway: Low glucose looks exactly like a stroke. Check glucose promptly, treat hypoglycemia first, then reassess.
questions.strategy: Fix the reversible cause before starting treatment for the scary diagnosis.

steps.detail: Glucose of 52 explains the symptoms.
A gives a clot buster before the mimic is ruled out.
D ignores swallow safety.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: A patient's spouse says she went to bed feeling fine at 2300 and woke him at 0630 unable to lift her right arm. What is her last known well time?

options.rationale: That is when the symptoms were found.
The last time she was known to be normal.

options.text: The time she arrived in the ED
options.rationale: Arrival time does not start the clock.

options.text: Unknown, so she cannot be treated
options.rationale: LKW is known: 2300.

questions.takeaway: Last known well is the last moment the patient was known to be normal, not when symptoms were discovered.
questions.strategy: For wake-up strokes, LKW is bedtime.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 0630 is discovery; 2300 is last known normal.
Arrival time and 'unknown' are both wrong here.

elimination.verdict: B is correct.

questions.stem: During an alteplase infusion, the patient reports a sudden severe headache and vomits. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.text: Give an antiemetic and continue the infusion.
options.rationale: These symptoms suggest bleeding in the brain.

options.text: Stop the infusion and notify the provider immediately.
options.rationale: Severe headache with nausea and vomiting may mean intracranial bleeding.

options.text: Slow the infusion rate by half.
options.rationale: A partial dose still risks worsening a bleed.

options.text: Recheck the vital signs in 15 minutes.
options.rationale: Waiting delays action on a possible bleed.
